# Causal Inference and Field Experiments {#sec-causal-inference}

Marketing decisions are causal claims in disguise. "Spend another dollar on
search advertising and we will earn three" is a statement about a counterfactual
world that did not happen—the sales the firm *would* have realized had it not
spent the dollar. A correlation between advertising and sales, however precisely
estimated, does not license that statement, because the firm chose how much to
advertise, and it chose to advertise more precisely where and when it expected to
sell more. The gap between *what we measure* (an association in observational
data) and *what we want to know* (the effect of an intervention we control) is the
central problem of this chapter, and of empirical marketing more broadly.

This chapter develops the modern toolkit for closing that gap. It begins with the
**potential-outcomes framework**, the language in which a causal effect is defined
before any estimator is chosen, and shows why the naive comparison of treated and
untreated units is biased by **selection**. It then treats randomized experiments
and online **A/B tests** as the benchmark that solves selection by design, and the
four leading **quasi-experimental** designs—**difference-in-differences (DiD)**,
**instrumental variables (IV)**, **regression discontinuity (RD)**, and the
**synthetic control method (SCM)**—as strategies for recovering causal effects
when randomization is infeasible. Each method is presented the same way: the
intuition first, then the estimator, then the identifying assumptions, and—most
important—*what breaks identification* and how a reader can tell. Throughout, the
running applications are the two domains where causal inference has reshaped
marketing practice: **advertising measurement** and **pricing**.

The stakes are not academic. A decade of large-scale field experiments has shown
that observational and even quasi-experimental estimates of advertising's return
can be off not by a few percent but by an order of magnitude, and sometimes carry
the wrong sign [@Lewis_2015; @gordon2019]. A marketing scientist who cannot
distinguish a credible causal estimate from an incredible one is a liability to
the firm. By the end of this chapter the reader will be able to state the
estimand, choose a design, defend its assumptions, implement the estimator in R,
and diagnose the most common failures.

## Semester arc {#sec-causal-semester-arc}

This chapter is organized as a fourteen-week doctoral seminar in causal inference
and field experiments, tuned to quantitative-marketing applications—advertising
measurement, pricing, promotions, and digital/platform experimentation. The arc
matches how the topic is taught in the empirical track of top programs (MIT,
Chicago Booth, Stanford GSB, Berkeley, Wharton, Columbia, Kellogg, NYU Stern, and
the economics and statistics departments marketing students cross-register into).
The single organizing question is *what makes the treatment as-good-as-randomly
assigned, conditional on what we observe and how we designed the study?*

The **first third** establishes the framework (potential outcomes and the
assignment mechanism), the gold standard (randomized experiments and large-scale
A/B testing), and the realistic case where randomization is absent (selection on
observables, and why regression is not magic). The ordering is deliberate:
students internalize the experimental ideal before judging how far an
observational design falls short of it. The **middle third** is a tour of
quasi-experimental designs, each motivated by a different source of
as-good-as-random variation: instrumental variables, difference-in-differences,
regression discontinuity, synthetic control, panel/event-study methods, and
matching/weighting. A recurring theme is that the past decade *re-litigated the
workhorses*—most dramatically the two-way fixed-effects DiD estimator, long the
default, shown to be badly biased under staggered adoption and heterogeneous
effects. The seminar treats this episode as the field's central methodological
cautionary tale: a method can be standard, published thousands of times, and still
wrong. The **final third** turns to the machine-learning and marketing-platform
frontier: ML for heterogeneous treatment effects; advertising measurement when
effects are tiny relative to sales noise; the experimental designs platforms
actually use (ghost ads, PSA holdouts, geo experiments); incrementality, pricing,
and targeting-policy evaluation; and the interference/spillover problems that break
SUTVA in marketplaces and social networks. The course closes on the question every
marketing dissertation must answer: *given that the effect is real but small and
the platform is non-stationary, what is the credible research design, and can it
scale?*

The standing textbooks for the whole course are Imbens and Rubin's *Causal
Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences* (Cambridge, 2015, the
potential-outcomes spine), Angrist and Pischke's *Mostly Harmless Econometrics*
(Princeton, 2009, the applied quasi-experimental workhorse), Cunningham's *Causal
Inference: The Mixtape* (Yale, 2021, a modern code-forward synthesis), and
Wooldridge's *Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data*, 2nd ed. (MIT,
2010, the panel/fixed-effects reference). Each weekly module below names its
**topic**, **subtopics**, **methods**, **key readings** (with DOI links and a
one-line rationale; foundational works are marked **[F]**, frontier works **[R]**),
and **central debate**. The detailed derivations, R simulations, and worked
marketing examples that follow the weekly map—the potential-outcomes algebra, the
A/B-power simulation, the DiD/IV/RD/SCM code, and the design-comparison table—are
the seminar's lab sessions; they are kept intact and cross-referenced from the
weeks they support.

### Week 1 — Potential Outcomes and the Assignment Mechanism {#sec-causal-week01}

**Topic.** [F] The Neyman–Rubin potential-outcomes model as the language in which a
causal effect is defined before any estimator is chosen.

**Subtopics.** The fundamental problem of causal inference; SUTVA; the estimands
(ATE, ATT, CATE); the assignment mechanism as the central object; "no causation
without manipulation"; causal versus predictive questions.

**Methods.** Writing an estimand precisely; distinguishing
estimand / identification / estimation / inference; recognizing when a question is
causal versus descriptive. Worked algebra in
@sec-causal-potential-outcomes below.

**Key readings.**

- Rubin, D. B. (1974). "Estimating Causal Effects of Treatments in Randomized and
  Nonrandomized Studies." *Journal of Educational Psychology* 66(5), 688–701.
  [doi:10.1037/h0037350](https://doi.org/10.1037/h0037350) — **[F]** the founding
  statement of the potential-outcomes framework.
- Holland, P. W. (1986). "Statistics and Causal Inference." *Journal of the
  American Statistical Association* 81(396), 945–960.
  [doi:10.1080/01621459.1986.10478354](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1986.10478354)
  — **[F]** formalizes the framework and the "no causation without manipulation"
  doctrine; the field's conceptual touchstone.
- Imbens, G. W. & Rubin, D. B. (2015). *Causal Inference for Statistics, Social,
  and Biomedical Sciences*, Part I. Cambridge University Press *(book)* — **[F]**
  potential outcomes and the assignment mechanism, in book length.

**Debate.** Is "manipulation" required for causality (what of immutable
characteristics)? ATE versus ATT versus policy-relevant estimands; design-based
versus model-based inference.

::: callout-note
## Controversy: the fast-food study that made design-based inference respectable

Marketing's causal-inference toolkit is borrowed almost entirely from economics,
and it was forged in a public argument worth knowing, because the moves both sides
made are the moves a referee will make about your identification strategy.

**1994 — the natural experiment.** Card and Krueger study employment at fast-food
restaurants either side of the New Jersey–Pennsylvania border after New Jersey
raised its minimum wage, and report no employment loss—against a strong theoretical
prior that it should fall.[^47-cardkrueger] The design is the point: a policy
boundary supplies the comparison, rather than a functional form.

**2000 — the data are attacked, not the logic.** @neumark2000comment reanalyze the
question using payroll records rather than the original telephone survey, and
report results pointing the other way. The critique is aimed squarely at
measurement: if your outcome is self-reported employment collected by phone,
your finding is only as good as that instrument.

**2000 — the reply, same issue.** @cardkrueger2000reply respond with a further
data source and maintain the original conclusion, while conceding what the payroll
data do and do not show.

**Why it belongs in this chapter.** Notice where the argument went. Nobody disputed
that a border discontinuity, if the data are sound, identifies something
interpretable. The fight moved immediately to *measurement*—which is where
design-based disputes almost always end up once the design itself is credible. That
is the standard your own difference-in-differences will be held to
(@sec-causal-week05): a referee who accepts your design will then ask where your
outcome variable came from, and "the platform's dashboard" is an answer with the
same structure as "a telephone survey."
:::

[^47-cardkrueger]: David Card and Alan B. Krueger (1994), "Minimum Wages and
Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania,"
*American Economic Review* 84(4), 772–793. The 1994 article predates DOI
assignment; the 2000 exchange it provoked is cited above by DOI.

### Week 2 — Randomized Experiments and A/B Testing at Scale {#sec-causal-week02}

**Topic.** [F]→[R] Randomization as the assignment mechanism that identifies the
ATE, scaled up to industrial web experimentation.

**Subtopics.** Fisher's sharp null and randomization inference versus Neyman's
repeated-sampling inference; covariate balance, stratification, and blocking;
CUPED-style variance reduction; the engineering of web experimentation,
sample-ratio mismatch, peeking/optional stopping, and the experimentation platform
as an organizational artifact.

**Methods.** Running Fisherian permutation tests; computing Neyman variance;
designing stratified/clustered assignment; variance reduction; diagnosing
sample-ratio mismatch. Lab: the A/B-power simulation in
@sec-causal-rct below (@fig-ab-power).

**Key readings.**

- Kohavi, R., Longbotham, R., Sommerfield, D. & Henne, R. M. (2009). "Controlled
  Experiments on the Web: Survey and Practical Guide." *Data Mining and Knowledge
  Discovery* 18(1), 140–181.
  [doi:10.1007/s10618-008-0114-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10618-008-0114-1) —
  **[R]** the practitioner canon for industrial-scale A/B testing; the pitfalls
  students will actually hit.
- Bojinov, I. & Shephard, N. (2019). "Time Series Experiments and Causal
  Estimands: Exact Randomization Tests and Trading." *Journal of the American
  Statistical Association* 114(528), 1665–1682.
  [doi:10.1080/01621459.2018.1527225](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2018.1527225)
  — **[R]** extends design-based randomization inference to single-unit,
  switchback-style time-series experiments (directly relevant to one-market
  pricing/ad tests).
- Imbens, G. W. & Rubin, D. B. (2015). *Causal Inference...*, Part II. Cambridge
  University Press *(book)* — **[F]** classical randomized experiments; Fisher and
  Neyman inference.
- Huch, E., Nail, S. A., Melconian, T., Vongsathorn, X. & Feinberg, F. (2026).
  "Overall Evaluation Criteria for A/B Tests: A Meta-Analytic Approach."
  *Marketing Science*, published online ahead of print.
  [doi:10.1287/mksc.2025.0164](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2025.0164) —
  **[R]** pools an archive of experiments to estimate each test's long-run
  effect from short-run metrics; method and replication in @sec-causal-oec.

**Debate.** Fisher versus Neyman inference; fixed-horizon versus
sequential/always-valid testing; how much can web A/B testing actually learn given
non-stationarity and short windows?

### Week 3 — Regression and Selection on Observables {#sec-causal-week03}

**Topic.** [F] The conditional-independence (unconfoundedness) assumption and what
regression actually estimates under it.

**Subtopics.** Regression as a weighting/comparison estimator and what it estimates
under heterogeneity; "bad controls" and collider bias; the overlap/common-support
condition; omitted-variable bias and sensitivity.

**Methods.** Specifying a credible conditioning set; drawing causal DAGs to spot
bad controls and colliders; checking overlap; OVB sensitivity bounds. The
selection-bias decomposition is derived in
@sec-causal-naive-comparison below, and @sec-causal-oster works an Oster bound
on published numbers.

::: callout-note
## Controversy: can matching recover an experimental answer?

This is the single most relevant economics dispute for anyone doing marketing
attribution, because it is the same question in different clothes: when you have
observational data and a conditioning set, can you recover what a randomized
experiment would have found?

**1986 — the benchmark, and the bad news.** LaLonde takes a randomized job-training
experiment, discards the experimental control group, substitutes non-experimental
comparison groups drawn from survey data, and applies the econometric estimators of
the day.[^47-lalonde] They do not recover the experimental answer. The estimates
vary widely with specification and comparison group, and an analyst without the
experimental benchmark would have had no way to know which was right.

**1999 — the optimistic reassessment.** @dehejia1999causal revisit the same data
with propensity-score methods and report that, with careful matching and attention
to overlap, the experimental estimate *can* be recovered. This result is
enormously influential and is a large part of why propensity-score matching spread
across the applied social sciences.

**2005 — the qualification.** @smithtodd2005matching ask, in their title, *Does
Matching Overcome LaLonde's Critique of Nonexperimental Estimators?* Their answer
is: not robustly. The favorable results are sensitive to the particular sample and
specification choices, and the performance degrades when those choices vary.

**What survives, and what it means for attribution.** The defensible reading is
that matching helps when the comparison group is drawn from the same population,
faces the same environment, and is compared on rich pre-treatment covariates
including the outcome's own history—and is unreliable otherwise. Notice that this
is the *same* conclusion the advertising literature reached independently
(@sec-advertising): observational methods benchmarked against experiments diverge,
and not with a constant bias one could correct. Two literatures, thirty years
apart, arriving at the same place is worth more than either alone.
:::

[^47-lalonde]: Robert J. LaLonde (1986), "Evaluating the Econometric Evaluations of
Training Programs with Experimental Data," *American Economic Review* 76(4),
604–620. The article predates DOI assignment; the reassessments it provoked are
cited above by DOI.

**Key readings.**

- Athey, S. & Imbens, G. W. (2017). "The State of Applied Econometrics: Causality
  and Policy Evaluation." *Journal of Economic Perspectives* 31(2), 3–32.
  [doi:10.1257/jep.31.2.3](https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.31.2.3) — **[R]** the modern
  map of identification strategies and where selection-on-observables sits among
  them; assigned as the course's strategic overview.
- Angrist, J. D. & Pischke, J.-S. (2009). *Mostly Harmless Econometrics*, ch. 3.
  Princeton University Press *(book)* — **[F]** regression and the
  conditional-independence assumption; the "bad control" problem.
- Imbens, G. W. & Rubin, D. B. (2015). *Causal Inference...*, Part III. Cambridge
  University Press *(book)* — **[F]** unconfoundedness and regression.

**Debate.** When is "control for everything" self-defeating? How much faith can
selection-on-observables ever earn without a design?

### Week 4 — Instrumental Variables {#sec-causal-week04}

**Topic.** [F] Recovering causal effects from an exogenous shifter of an endogenous
treatment.

**Subtopics.** The IV/2SLS estimator; the LATE theorem and the
monotonicity/exclusion/relevance assumptions; compliers and what LATE is the
effect *for*; weak instruments; judge/examiner and shift-share designs; IV in
marketing (price endogeneity, demand estimation).

**Methods.** 2SLS and its LATE interpretation; first-stage *F* / weak-IV
diagnostics; reasoning about exclusion and monotonicity in a real application. Lab:
the demand-estimation IV simulation in @sec-causal-iv below.

**Key readings.**

- Imbens, G. W. & Angrist, J. D. (1994). "Identification and Estimation of Local
  Average Treatment Effects." *Econometrica* 62(2), 467–475.
  [doi:10.2307/2951620](https://doi.org/10.2307/2951620) — **[F]** the LATE
  theorem; redefines what IV identifies under heterogeneity.
- Angrist, J. D., Imbens, G. W. & Rubin, D. B. (1996). "Identification of Causal
  Effects Using Instrumental Variables." *Journal of the American Statistical
  Association* 91(434), 444–455.
  [doi:10.1080/01621459.1996.10476902](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1996.10476902)
  — **[F]** embeds IV in potential outcomes; the canonical compliers/defiers
  exposition.
- Angrist, J. D. & Pischke, J.-S. (2009). *Mostly Harmless Econometrics*, ch. 4.
  Princeton University Press *(book)* — **[F]** applied IV and weak-instrument
  diagnostics.

**Debate.** Is LATE a "policy-relevant" estimand or an artifact of the instrument?
Are most instruments' exclusion restrictions defensible?

### Week 5 — Difference-in-Differences I: Foundations and the 2×2 {#sec-causal-week05}

**Topic.** [F] The canonical 2×2 DiD and the parallel-trends assumption.

**Subtopics.** Event-study/pre-trend plots; clustered and serially correlated
standard errors; placebo and pre-trend tests; DiD for marketing launches, entry,
and policy/regulatory shocks.

**Methods.** Building event-study plots; testing parallel pre-trends; clustering
and wild-cluster bootstrap; placebo tests. Lab: the DiD panel simulation in
@sec-causal-did below.

**Key readings.**

- Bertrand, M., Duflo, E. & Mullainathan, S. (2004). "How Much Should We Trust
  Differences-in-Differences Estimates?" *The Quarterly Journal of Economics*
  119(1), 249–275.
  [doi:10.1162/003355304772839588](https://doi.org/10.1162/003355304772839588) —
  **[F]** exposes serial-correlation underestimation of DiD standard errors; the
  inference cautionary tale.
- Card, D. & Krueger, A. B. (2000). "Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of
  the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania: Reply." *American Economic
  Review* 90(5), 1397–1420.
  [doi:10.1257/aer.90.5.1397](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.90.5.1397) — **[F]** the
  verified record for the canonical minimum-wage DiD program; the design that made
  DiD a default tool. (The original Card & Krueger 1994 *AER* article is *(DOI to
  verify)*.)
- Angrist, J. D. & Pischke, J.-S. (2009). *Mostly Harmless Econometrics*, ch. 5.
  Princeton University Press *(book)* — **[F]** DiD and fixed effects, the
  classical treatment.

**Debate.** Is parallel trends testable, or only falsifiable on pre-periods? How
much should inference (not point estimates) drive DiD credibility?

### Week 6 — Difference-in-Differences II: Staggered Adoption and the TWFE Critique {#sec-causal-week06}

**Topic.** [R] The field's central recent methodological episode: why two-way
fixed-effects DiD is biased under staggered timing and heterogeneous effects, and
the family of robust estimators that replaced it.

**Subtopics.** "Forbidden comparisons" and negative weights; decomposition
diagnostics; the new robust estimators (group-time ATTs, interaction-weighted event
studies, imputation); choosing among them; honest pre-trends.

**Methods.** Running Goodman-Bacon decompositions; estimating the
Callaway–Sant'Anna, Sun–Abraham, and Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess estimators and
reconciling them; honest pre-trend (HonestDiD-style) sensitivity. The TWFE failure
is introduced in the DiD discussion at @sec-causal-did.

  Timing." *Journal of Econometrics* 225(2), 254–277.
  [doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2021.03.014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2021.03.014)
  — **[R]** the decomposition showing TWFE is a weighted average of all 2×2s,
  including "forbidden" already-treated comparisons.

  [doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2020.09.006](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2020.09.006)

  [doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2023.03.008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2023.03.008)

### Week 7 — Regression Discontinuity Designs {#sec-causal-week07}

**Topic.** [F]→[R] Identifying the local effect at a known assignment threshold,
with modern robust inference.

**Subtopics.** Sharp and fuzzy RDD; continuity-based versus local-randomization

tests (density discontinuity); RDD in marketing (loyalty-tier thresholds, ad-auction
reserve prices, eligibility cutoffs).

**Methods.** Local-polynomial estimation; MSE-optimal and CER-optimal bandwidths;

### Week 8 — Synthetic Control {#sec-causal-week08}

**Topic.** [F]→[R] Constructing a single treated unit's counterfactual from a
weighted average of donors.

**Subtopics.** The synthetic-control estimator as a data-driven weighted comparison;
placebo/permutation inference; pre-treatment fit and donor-pool selection;
extensions—generalized synthetic control (interactive fixed effects), synthetic
DiD, and Bayesian structural-time-series "CausalImpact" (geo/ad applications).

**Methods.** Constructing donor pools and weights; permutation/placebo inference;
choosing among SC / synthetic DiD / gsynth / CausalImpact for a marketing case.

## The Potential-Outcomes Framework {#sec-causal-potential-outcomes}

The foundational move of modern causal inference is to define the effect of a
treatment *for each unit* before worrying about how to estimate it. Following the
Neyman–Rubin potential-outcomes model, let $D_i \in \{0,1\}$ denote whether unit
$i$ (a consumer, a store, a geographic market, a designated market area) receives
a treatment—an ad campaign, a price cut, a new feature. Associate with each unit
two **potential outcomes**: $Y_i(1)$, the outcome that *would* occur under
treatment, and $Y_i(0)$, the outcome that *would* occur under control. The
**unit-level treatment effect** is their difference,

$$
\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0).
$$ {#eq-unit-effect}

The defining difficulty—the *fundamental problem of causal inference*—is that for
any unit we observe only one potential outcome. The realized outcome is

$$
Y_i = D_i\,Y_i(1) + (1 - D_i)\,Y_i(0),
$$ {#eq-switching}

so the other potential outcome is a **counterfactual** that is missing by
construction. We never see $\tau_i$ for any single unit. Causal inference is
therefore, at root, a **missing-data problem**, and progress comes from estimating
*averages* of $\tau_i$ over populations rather than the unit-level effects
themselves.

> A causal effect is a comparison of two states of the world that differ only in
> the treatment: the outcome we observe under the treatment a unit received, and
> the outcome that same unit would have realized under the treatment it did not
> receive. Because only one of these is ever observed, every causal estimate rests
> on an assumption that makes the missing outcome recoverable from the data.

The chief estimand is the **average treatment effect (ATE)**,
$\tau_{\text{ATE}} = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]$, the expected effect of moving a
randomly chosen unit from control to treatment. Two relatives matter in practice.
The **average treatment effect on the treated (ATT)**,
$\tau_{\text{ATT}} = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1]$, is the effect for
the units that actually received treatment—the relevant quantity when asking
whether a campaign *that ran* paid off. The **conditional average treatment effect
(CATE)**, $\tau(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid \mathbf{X}_i =
\mathbf{x}]$, is the effect for a subpopulation with covariates $\mathbf{x}$, the
target of modern heterogeneous-treatment-effect and targeting
methods.[^estimand-first]

[^estimand-first]: A discipline this chapter enforces: name the estimand *before*
choosing a method. Much confusion in applied marketing arises from estimating one
quantity (say, an ATT among self-selected adopters) and interpreting it as
another (the ATE the firm would obtain by treating everyone). The two coincide
only under constant effects.

### Why the Naive Comparison Fails {#sec-causal-naive-comparison}

The intuitive estimator of a treatment effect is the difference in mean outcomes
between treated and untreated units, $\hat\Delta = \bar Y_{D=1} - \bar Y_{D=0}$.
Decomposing its probability limit exposes exactly why it is biased. Adding and
subtracting $\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1]$ gives

$$
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 0]}_{\text{naive difference}}
= \underbrace{\tau_{\text{ATT}}}_{\text{causal effect}}
+ \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0]}_{\text{selection bias}}.
$$ {#eq-selection-bias}

The second term is **selection bias**: the difference in the *baseline* (untreated)
outcome between the groups that did and did not get treated. It is zero only if
treated and untreated units would have looked the same absent treatment. In
marketing they almost never do. A firm targets ads at consumers already inclined
to buy; it cuts prices on products whose demand is already softening; loyal
customers self-select into a rewards program. In each case
$\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] \neq \mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0]$, and the
naive difference confounds the effect of the treatment with the reasons the unit
was treated. The remainder of this chapter is a catalogue of designs that drive
the selection-bias term to zero—by randomization, or by an assumption that makes
the untreated a valid stand-in for the treated counterfactual.

Two assumptions are maintained throughout unless stated otherwise. **SUTVA** (the
stable-unit-treatment-value assumption) requires that one unit's potential outcomes
not depend on other units' treatment assignments (no interference) and that there
be a single version of the treatment. SUTVA is violated by spillovers—a price
promotion at one store cannibalizing a neighbor, an ad shown to one household
influencing another through word of mouth—which is why experimental units in
marketing are often *geographies* rather than individuals. **Overlap** (positivity)
requires $0 < \Pr(D_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{X}_i) < 1$ for all covariate values, so that
comparable treated and control units exist at every $\mathbf{x}$. Overlap is often
treated as the easy half of strong ignorability, but algorithmic allocation can
violate it by design. An ad auction that always awards an impression to the top
bidder gives many users a propensity of exactly zero or one. DML and inverse-propensity
weighting then recover the effect only for users whose assignment was genuinely
random, even though the logged allocation rule makes assignment unconfounded
[@rafieian2026overlap] (see @sec-adv-overlap).

## Randomized Experiments and A/B Tests {#sec-causal-rct}

Randomization is the gold standard because it eliminates selection bias *by
construction* rather than by assumption. If treatment $D_i$ is assigned
independently of the potential outcomes—$\{Y_i(0), Y_i(1)\} \perp D_i$—then the
untreated group is, in expectation, a valid counterfactual for the treated group:
$\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0]$. The
selection-bias term in @eq-selection-bias vanishes, and the difference in means is
unbiased for the ATE,

$$
\hat\tau_{\text{ATE}} = \bar Y_{D=1} - \bar Y_{D=0}.
$$ {#eq-rct-estimator}

The identifying assumption—independence of assignment and potential
outcomes—holds because the experimenter, not the units, controls $D_i$. This is
the single most important idea in the chapter: randomization does not make treated
and control units *identical*, it makes them *exchangeable in expectation*, which
is all that @eq-rct-estimator requires.

In the digital economy this logic is operationalized at enormous scale as the
**A/B test** (online controlled experiment): users arriving at a site are
randomly bucketed into a control arm seeing the incumbent experience and one or
more treatment arms seeing a variant, and a metric—conversion, revenue per
session, retention—is compared across arms. The mechanics are simple; the
discipline is in the design. Three issues dominate practice.

**Power and the minimum detectable effect.** An experiment that cannot detect the
effect sizes that matter is worse than no experiment, because it invites the
fallacy of accepting the null. For a two-arm test of a mean with equal allocation,
the sample size per arm needed to detect a true difference $\delta$ at
significance level $\alpha$ and power $1-\beta$ is approximately

$$
n \;\approx\; \frac{2\,(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2\,\sigma^2}{\delta^2},
$$ {#eq-power}

where $\sigma^2$ is the outcome variance and $z_p$ the standard-normal quantile.
The quadratic dependence on $\delta$ is the crux of advertising measurement: sales
are so volatile relative to advertising's effect that the required sample is often
larger than even large firms can muster, a point developed below.

**The randomization unit and interference.** When treating a user can affect other
users—social spillovers, marketplace competition for the same inventory, supply
constraints—unit-level randomization violates SUTVA and biases the estimate.
Cluster-randomizing at the level of the interference (markets, regions, social
clusters) restores validity at the cost of effective sample size.

**Peeking and the validity of the stopping rule.** Repeatedly testing a running
experiment and stopping the first time $p < 0.05$ inflates the false-positive rate
far above the nominal level. Either fix the sample size in advance, or adopt a
sequential procedure (always-valid $p$-values, group-sequential boundaries) whose
error guarantee survives continuous monitoring.

set.seed(47)

# Data-generating process: a latent 'propensity' drives BOTH self-selection
# into treatment (observationally) AND the baseline outcome -> confounding.
make_population <- function(n, true_tau = 0.20) {
  propensity <- rnorm(n)                       # latent buying inclination
  Y0 <- 0.50 + 0.40 * propensity + rnorm(n)    # untreated potential outcome
  Y1 <- Y0 + true_tau                          # constant treatment effect
  data.frame(propensity, Y0, Y1)
}

# (1) OBSERVATIONAL: high-propensity users self-select into treatment.
n <- 4000
pop <- make_population(n)
D_obs <- as.integer(pop$propensity + rnorm(n) > 0)   # selection on propensity
Y_obs <- ifelse(D_obs == 1, pop$Y1, pop$Y0)
naive <- mean(Y_obs[D_obs == 1]) - mean(Y_obs[D_obs == 0])

# (2) RANDOMIZED: assignment independent of potential outcomes.
rct_estimate <- function(n_per_arm = 1000, true_tau = 0.20) {
  p <- make_population(2 * n_per_arm, true_tau)
  D <- rep(0:1, each = n_per_arm)
  D <- sample(D)                               # random assignment
  Y <- ifelse(D == 1, p$Y1, p$Y0)
  mean(Y[D == 1]) - mean(Y[D == 0])
}

#> Mean of randomized estimates:   0.201  (unbiased)

hist(rct_draws, breaks = 40, col = "grey80", border = "white",

### Advertising Measurement: The Hard Case for Experiments {#sec-causal-ad-measurement}

Advertising is the canonical setting where experiments are both essential and
difficult. The difficulty is statistical, and @eq-power explains it. The effect of
a typical online display campaign on purchase probability is small in absolute
terms, while individual purchasing is enormously variable; substituting realistic
magnitudes into @eq-power implies that detecting advertising's true return on
investment with confidence can require *millions* of randomized users—more than
many campaigns ever reach [@Lewis_2015]. Lewis and Rao show that even well-powered
experiments deliver confidence intervals on ROI so wide that firms cannot
distinguish a profitable campaign from a money-losing one, and that the
observational regressions firms typically run fare far worse.

How much worse is documented by large-scale comparisons. Across digital
advertising experiments at scale, observational methods—matching, regression
adjustment, propensity scores—routinely yield estimates that diverge sharply from
the experimental benchmark, frequently overstating effects by large multiples and
occasionally reversing their sign, because no set of observed covariates fully
captures why a platform showed a given user a given ad [@gordon2019]. The lesson
is not that observational methods are useless but that, in advertising, the
selection-bias term in @eq-selection-bias is large relative to the effect itself,
so even small failures of the conditional-independence assumption swamp the signal.
A recurrent culprit is **activity bias**: users who are online and active are both
more likely to be served (and to "see") an ad and more likely to convert for
reasons unrelated to the ad, manufacturing a spurious correlation that
intention-to-treat experimental designs avoid [@lewis2011].

These findings reframe the practitioner's task. The question is rarely "what is
the point estimate of ROI?" but "is my experiment powered to answer the decision I
face?"—and often the honest answer is to redesign the test (larger, geo-based, or
focused on an intermediate outcome) rather than to trust an underpowered or
observational number.

A constructive answer to the scaling problem treats each experiment as one labelled
observation rather than as a one-off verdict. @gordon2026pie train a model on 2,226
Meta experiments to predict a campaign's incremental conversions per dollar from
campaign aggregates (the test group's conversion rate, its exposure rate,
last-click counts) and apply it to campaigns run without a control group. The
features would be bad controls in a user-level causal model, because they are
outcomes of the campaign; in a campaign-level prediction model they are legitimate,
because the experiments, not the features, carry the identification. The
distinction between *identifying* an effect and *predicting* one that has already
been identified elsewhere is developed, with a replication of the paper's
simulations, in @sec-adv-pie.

### Born or Made? Field Data Plus a Randomized Experience Manipulation {#sec-causal-born-or-made}

Advertising is the case where the selection term in @eq-selection-bias swamps the effect.
A common marketing variant is subtler: the treatment is an *experience* the customer
chooses, and the question is whether the experience changes later behavior or merely
reveals who the customer already was. @kim2026customization pose exactly this question about
product customization. In a retailer's transaction records, customers who customize once are
more likely to customize again, and they spend more, visit more often, and buy more items.
Write $D_i = 1$ for "customized at least once" and $Y_i$ for later customization or spend.
The naive contrast then adds the causal effect of the experience to a selection term,
$\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0]$, which is the difference
in later behavior that an inherent taste for customizing would produce even without the
experience. Transaction data alone cannot separate "born" customizers from "made" ones.

The paper's multimethod answer, sketched in @fig-ci-born-made, adds longitudinal
experiments that randomize the experience itself. Some participants are assigned to
customize and others to choose from a *matched* set of ready-made products, and later
choices are tracked. The matched set is the design detail that matters. Comparing
customization with a generic or worse product would mix the effect of the customizing
experience with the effect of getting a better-fitting product. Matching the choice set
keeps the comparison on the experience. Because assignment is random, the inherent
preference is balanced across arms in expectation (the dashed path in the figure no longer
reaches treatment), and the difference in later customization identifies the effect of the
experience. The authors find that an initial customization experience significantly raises
the subsequent likelihood of customizing, with favorable downstream outcomes for customer
and retailer, so at least part of the field correlation is a causal journey effect rather
than pure sorting.

The design also shows what each half of the evidence buys. The field data supply
external validity: real customers, real money, and a nine-year horizon long enough to see
repeat behavior. They are weak on identification. The experiments supply identification
and are weaker on external validity, because the participants, products, and stakes are
the experimenters' rather than the retailer's. Neither half alone gives the quantity a
retailer most wants, which is how much of the observed customizer premium would appear among
customers who customize only because the firm nudged them. That is the question
@sec-clv-customization-journey takes up, and the answer depends on how closely the
experimental experience matches the field intervention. (Only the published abstract was
accessible when this section was written. It does not report the field sample size, how the
transaction analysis adjusts for self-selection, or the number and sizes of the experiments,
so this description stays at the level of the design logic.)


### Policy Lotteries and the Estimand You Actually Want {#sec-causal-policy-lottery}

Not every randomization is run by a researcher. Governments allocate scarce rights by
lottery—visas, permits, school seats, subsidy slots—and those lotteries are experiments
whose treatment is a *policy*, which is often the treatment a decision-maker cares about
and rarely the one a study estimates. @clemens2026lowskill make the distinction sharply.
The dominant identification strategy in their literature instruments for immigrant
presence with historical settlement patterns, which identifies a local average treatment
effect of varying immigrant *supply* regardless of current demand. The policy question is
different: what happens when a quota binds on firms that want to hire *now*? That is a
policy-relevant treatment effect, and it is recovered by the quota's own randomization—the
H-2B visa lottery—rather than by an instrument built from history.

Three features of the design are worth importing into marketing work whenever an
allocation rule contains randomness. The randomization is at the level of the
decision-making unit (the firm), not the individual, so the estimates speak to firm-level
adjustment rather than to worker-level exposure. Hypotheses, subsample tests, and
predicted signs were committed to a **pre-analysis plan** before data collection, which
converts the heterogeneity analysis from exploration into a test. And the outcome data
come from a purpose-built survey of winners and losers rather than from whatever
administrative file happened to exist, with prespecified checks on item and global
nonresponse. Marketing has more of these opportunities than it uses: oversubscribed beta
programs, capacity-rationed loyalty perks, lotteried event invitations, and regulator-run
license allocations all embed randomization that a firm can exploit without running an
experiment of its own. @sec-sw-decomposition treats the same paper as a template for
writing up a mechanism rather than an average.


The same logic applies when the randomized policy is an enforcement action rather
than an allocation. @fan2026enforcement use China's randomized pre-IPO on-site
inspection program, under which the securities regulator draws a random subset of
IPO applicants for intensive inspection of their books, to estimate the causal effect
of proactive public enforcement on the financial reporting quality of applicants in a
setting with weak institutional oversight. Selected applicants end up with better
reporting, largely because inspection screens out firms with questionable
disclosures. The larger effect is deterrence: later applicants, who were never drawn,
submit higher-quality reports because they might be. The cost is that some firms that
would have merited approval are rejected. Two features carry over to marketing
settings. Randomizing the point of enforcement identifies the policy-relevant effect
of scrutiny itself, free of the targeting that makes ordinary audits uninformative
about deterrence, and the deterrence result is a spillover onto untreated units of
exactly the kind @sec-policy-spillovers warns will contaminate a naive comparison of
inspected firms with their uninspected peers. (Only the published abstract was
accessible when this section was written; the magnitudes are in the paper.)

Firms run policy experiments too, and the same point about estimands applies.
@fang2026returnless randomized nearly one million customers of a global e-commerce
platform between an AI-decided, returnless partial refund and the standard process of
shipping the item back for a full refund. The treatment arm changes three things at
once: who decides, whether the item comes back, and how much is refunded. The
experiment therefore identifies the effect of the policy as it would be deployed, not
the effect of any single component, and the deployment effect is the quantity the
platform's decision turns on. The outcomes are chosen the same way. Refund payouts,
processing costs, later purchasing, and strategic claiming each enter the platform's
payoff, and the paper reports all of them rather than a single headline metric
(@sec-sw-decomposition).

## Overall Evaluation Criteria: Learning Across A/B Tests {#sec-causal-oec}

A single A/B test answers a narrow question well: did this variant move this
metric over these two weeks? The decision the firm faces is wider. It wants to know
whether the variant raises long-run value, and the metrics that measure long-run
value (six-month revenue, retention, closed transactions) are slow and noisy, while
the metrics that are fast and precise (clicks, form fills, sessions) are only
proxies. Practitioners resolve the tension with an **overall evaluation criterion**
(OEC): one number, built from short-run metrics, that is supposed to track long-run
value [@kohavi2020trustworthy]. In most firms the OEC is a weighted sum whose weights
were negotiated in a meeting.

@huch2026oec replace the meeting with a model. Their observation is that a firm that
has run hundreds of experiments already owns the data needed to learn how short-run
effects map to long-run effects: every past test whose long-run outcome has matured
is one observation on that mapping. The method is a multivariate random-effects
meta-analysis, the tool biostatisticians built to validate surrogate endpoints in
clinical trials [@dersimonian1986meta; @buyse2000surrogate], applied to an archive of
A/B tests. It needs only two summaries per test, a vector of effect estimates and
its covariance matrix, and it returns for every test, finished or still running, a
posterior distribution for the long-run effect. This section sets out the full
method, reports what the authors find in 190 tests at Zillow, and replicates the
estimators in R.

### Setup: what the archive must contain {#sec-causal-oec-setup}

Index past experiments by $t = 1, \dots, T$. Each test reports a vector of estimated
treatment effects on $p$ metrics, $\mathbf z_t \in \mathbb R^p$, together with an
estimate of its sampling covariance $\boldsymbol\Sigma_t$. With a difference in
means, $\mathbf z_t = \bar{\mathbf m}_{t1} - \bar{\mathbf m}_{t0}$ and
$\boldsymbol\Sigma_t = \mathbf S_{t1}/n_{t1} + \mathbf S_{t0}/n_{t0}$, where
$\mathbf S_{ta}$ is the sample covariance matrix of the metrics in arm $a$. Any
estimator will do, including a covariate-adjusted one such as CUPED
[@deng2013cuped], as long as two conditions hold. The estimate must be
approximately Gaussian around the true effect vector $\boldsymbol\mu_t$, and the
covariance estimate must be consistent, so that it can be treated as known:

$$
\mathbf z_t \mid \boldsymbol\mu_t \;\sim\; \mathcal N\!\left(\boldsymbol\mu_t, \boldsymbol\Sigma_t\right).
$$ {#eq-oec-likelihood}

The only new bookkeeping relative to standard practice is the off-diagonal part of
$\boldsymbol\Sigma_t$. A platform that analyzes one metric at a time already
computes the diagonal; the method also needs the covariances between metrics, and
it needs metric definitions and measurement windows that are the same across tests.
In the Zillow application these summaries shrink the data from billions of
customer-level rows to a few hundred.

Split the metrics into two groups, $\mathbf z_t = (\mathbf y_t^\top, \mathbf
x_t^\top)^\top$, with true effects $\boldsymbol\mu_t = (\boldsymbol\mu_{yt}^\top,
\boldsymbol\mu_{xt}^\top)^\top$. The $r$ metrics in $\mathbf y_t$ are the key
performance indicators the business cares about. The $q$ metrics in $\mathbf x_t$
are proxies. Both are estimated effects on post-treatment outcomes; neither is a
covariate. The analyst then defines the target as a function of the *true* KPI
effects,

$$
\text{OEC}_t \;=\; f\!\left(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt}\right),
$$ {#eq-oec-definition}

and the three examples in the paper cover most uses. With one KPI, such as revenue
per customer over six months, $f$ is the identity. With revenue split by line of
business, $f(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt}) = \mathbf 1_r^\top \boldsymbol\mu_{yt}$ adds the
lines up. With a conversion funnel whose stage-$j$ effect is a log ratio of
conditional conversion rates, $f(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt}) = \exp(\mathbf 1_r^\top
\boldsymbol\mu_{yt}) - 1$ is the lift at the bottom of the funnel. The funnel case
shows that the proxies need not be measured earlier than the KPI. Bottom-of-funnel
events are rare, so their effects are estimated imprecisely even when the window is
the same, and the upper-funnel metrics lend them precision.

Defining the OEC as a function of true effects is the step that separates this
framework from an OEC by committee. The target is stated in business terms and never
changes. What the model learns is how much each proxy says about it.

### The benchmark: one test at a time {#sec-causal-oec-naive}

The estimator every platform already computes is the plug-in

$$
\widehat{\text{OEC}}_t = f(\mathbf y_t),
\qquad
\frac{\widehat{\text{OEC}}_t - \text{OEC}_t}
     {\sqrt{f'(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt})^\top \boldsymbol\Sigma_{yyt}\, f'(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt})}}
\;\xrightarrow{d}\; \mathcal N(0, 1),
$$ {#eq-oec-naive}

with the standard error from the delta method. The authors call it the naive
method. It ignores the proxies and it ignores every other test. It is unbiased for
each test taken alone, and it has two defects that matter in practice. Its
intervals are wide, because the KPIs are noisy. And it is biased *conditional on
being selected*: a firm ships the variants whose estimates are large and positive,
and the estimates that clear that bar are disproportionately the ones whose noise
happened to be positive. The summed "impact" of a year of shipped winners is
therefore overstated, by regression to the mean.

### The meta-analytic model {#sec-causal-oec-model}

The fix is one added assumption. The true effect vectors of the tests in the archive
are independent draws from a common distribution,

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_t \;\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\; P_{\boldsymbol\theta},
\qquad \boldsymbol\theta \sim p(\boldsymbol\theta \mid \boldsymbol\theta_0),
$$ {#eq-oec-prior}

with a hyperprior on the unknown $\boldsymbol\theta$. This is the standard
exchangeability assumption of meta-analysis. Univariate versions were already in
use for online experiments, for example to show that the distribution of true
effects at Bing has fat tails [@azevedo2020fattails]. Because $\boldsymbol\mu_t$ is
a vector, $P_{\boldsymbol\theta}$ carries more than a location and a spread: it
carries the correlations between true effects on different metrics across
experiments, and those correlations are what allow one metric to stand in for
another. @fig-oec-model draws the model.

Why is the posterior the right estimator? Take squared-error loss and average it
over both the sampling noise and the draw of $\boldsymbol\mu_t$ from
$P_{\boldsymbol\theta}$. The estimator that minimizes this Bayes risk is the
posterior mean of $f(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt})$ given $\mathbf z_t$. With
$\boldsymbol\theta$ unknown, the fully Bayesian version integrates over its
posterior, and in practice that is done by applying $f$ to Markov chain Monte Carlo
draws of $\boldsymbol\mu_{yt}$.

It helps to be exact about what has been assumed and what has not. Surrogate-index
methods [@athey2026surrogateindex; @yang2024longterm] work with individual-level
data and assume that the long-run outcome is independent of treatment given the
surrogates, so that the surrogates capture every channel through which treatment
acts. The meta-analytic model makes no such claim about mechanisms. It replaces the
causal surrogacy assumption with a statistical one about the *population of
experiments*, and it measures the strength of surrogacy empirically, as a
cross-experiment correlation, instead of assuming it. The cost is that
@eq-oec-prior must be credible. It is most credible for many closely related tests
on one platform and one customer population. It fails when tests interfere with
each other, when the archive mixes domains, or when something observable about a
test predicts its effect. The authors' remedy for the last case is metaregression:
let the effect distribution depend on test-level covariates $\mathbf w_t$ (platform,
intervention type, duration, or summaries of $\boldsymbol\Sigma_t$ if strong tests
are stopped early) and require exchangeability only conditional on them. The
assumption has observable consequences, so it can be checked with posterior
predictive tests of dependence between $\boldsymbol\mu_t$ and test metadata.

### Three priors for the distribution of effects {#sec-causal-oec-priors}

**Gaussian.** With $\boldsymbol\mu_t \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\eta,
\boldsymbol\Omega)$, the posterior of a test's true effects given
$\boldsymbol\theta = (\boldsymbol\eta, \boldsymbol\Omega)$ is available in closed
form:

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_t \mid \mathbf z_t, \boldsymbol\theta \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\eta_t, \boldsymbol\Omega_t),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\Omega_t = \left(\boldsymbol\Omega^{-1} + \boldsymbol\Sigma_t^{-1}\right)^{-1},
\qquad
\boldsymbol\eta_t = \boldsymbol\Omega_t\left(\boldsymbol\Omega^{-1}\boldsymbol\eta + \boldsymbol\Sigma_t^{-1}\mathbf z_t\right).
$$ {#eq-oec-blup}

The posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the archive's mean effect and
the test's own estimate. It is the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) of
$\boldsymbol\mu_t$, which makes it the benchmark for any OEC that is linear in the
metrics, including a committee's weighted sum. Two properties follow from
@eq-oec-blup. As a test grows, $\boldsymbol\Sigma_t \to \mathbf 0$ and the BLUP
converges to the naive estimate, so a large test is left alone. And because
$\boldsymbol\Omega$ has off-diagonal terms, a precise proxy estimate moves the
posterior for a noisy KPI.

The second property gives the method its most practical use. Suppose only some
metrics have been observed, $\mathbf A \mathbf z_t$ for a selection matrix $\mathbf
A$, because the long-run window has not closed. The posterior becomes

$$
\boldsymbol\Omega_t = \left[\boldsymbol\Omega^{-1} + \mathbf A^\top\!\left(\mathbf A \boldsymbol\Sigma_t \mathbf A^\top\right)^{-1}\!\mathbf A\right]^{-1},
\qquad
\boldsymbol\eta_t = \boldsymbol\Omega_t\left[\boldsymbol\Omega^{-1}\boldsymbol\eta + \mathbf A^\top\!\left(\mathbf A \boldsymbol\Sigma_t \mathbf A^\top\right)^{-1}\!\mathbf A \mathbf z_t\right],
$$ {#eq-oec-missing}

which is a posterior for the long-run effect of a test whose long-run outcome does
not exist yet. The same expression handles a metric that a given test could not
track. The requirement is that the missingness is unrelated to the effects.

**Student-t.** True effects in online experiments have more large outliers than a
Gaussian allows. Replacing the prior with a multivariate Student-t,
$\boldsymbol\mu_t \sim \mathcal T(\boldsymbol\eta, \boldsymbol\Omega, \gamma)$,
shrinks a surprising estimate less. The posterior mean is no longer linear in
$\mathbf z_t$.

**Dirichlet process mixture (DPM).** The most flexible option drops the parametric
family. Tests belong to latent clusters, each with its own Gaussian, and the number
of clusters is inferred:

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_t \mid c_t \sim \mathcal N\!\left(\boldsymbol\eta_{c_t}, \boldsymbol\Omega_{c_t}\right),
\qquad
c_t \mid \boldsymbol\pi \sim \text{Categorical}(\boldsymbol\pi),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\pi \sim \text{GEM}(\alpha_0),
\qquad
(\boldsymbol\eta_k, \boldsymbol\Omega_k) \sim G_0 ,
$$ {#eq-oec-dpm}

with a Gaussian-inverse-Wishart base measure $G_0$ and a concentration parameter
$\alpha_0$ that governs how readily new clusters form. A test is now shrunk toward
the center of the cluster it most plausibly belongs to, not toward the grand mean.
The clusters are also a finding in their own right, because the model sees only
$(\mathbf z_t, \boldsymbol\Sigma_t)$ and still groups tests by the profile of their
effects.

### Measuring surrogacy {#sec-causal-oec-surrogacy}

The fitted $\boldsymbol\Omega$ answers a question that OEC committees argue about:
how good are the proxies? Following @buyse2000surrogate, the strength of the
proxies for the summed OEC is the share of cross-test variance in the OEC that the
proxy effects explain,

$$
R^2 \;=\; \frac{\mathbf 1_r^\top \boldsymbol\Omega_{yx}\boldsymbol\Omega_{xx}^{-1}\boldsymbol\Omega_{xy}\mathbf 1_r}
               {\mathbf 1_r^\top \boldsymbol\Omega_{yy}\mathbf 1_r}.
$$ {#eq-oec-r2}

A second set of diagnostics says where the precision comes from. Let $v_{0t} =
\mathbf u^\top \boldsymbol\Sigma_t \mathbf u$ be the naive variance of the OEC,
with $\mathbf u = (\mathbf 1_r^\top, \mathbf 0_q^\top)^\top$; let $v_{zt} = \mathbf
u^\top \boldsymbol\Omega_t \mathbf u$ be the posterior variance from
@eq-oec-blup; and let $v_{yt} = \mathbf 1_r^\top(\boldsymbol\Omega_{yy}^{-1} +
\boldsymbol\Sigma_{yyt}^{-1})^{-1}\mathbf 1_r$ be the posterior variance from a
meta-analysis that throws the proxies away. Then

$$
\underbrace{\frac{v_{zt}}{v_{0t}}}_{\text{TVR}_t}
\;=\;
\underbrace{\frac{v_{yt}}{v_{0t}}}_{\text{PVR}_t}
\times
\underbrace{\frac{v_{zt}}{v_{yt}}}_{\text{SVR}_t}.
$$ {#eq-oec-tvr}

The total variance ratio has a direct cost interpretation: to match the posterior
variance with the naive method, the test would need $1/\text{TVR}_t$ times as many
customers. The prior variance ratio is the part due to shrinking the KPIs toward
what the archive says is plausible. The surrogacy variance ratio is the further
gain from the proxies. Computing the three for each candidate proxy is a principled
way to decide which metrics belong in $\mathbf x_t$. Under the DPM the same
quantities are computed with each test's cluster covariance and averaged.

### Estimation {#sec-causal-oec-estimation}

All three models are fitted by collapsed Gibbs sampling. The Gaussian sampler
cycles through three blocks, with priors $\boldsymbol\eta \sim \mathcal
N(\boldsymbol\eta_0, \boldsymbol\Phi)$ and $\boldsymbol\Omega \sim \mathcal
W^{-1}(\boldsymbol\Psi, \nu)$:

1. Draw $\boldsymbol\Omega$ from $\mathcal W^{-1}\big(\boldsymbol\Psi + \sum_t
   (\boldsymbol\mu_t - \boldsymbol\eta)(\boldsymbol\mu_t - \boldsymbol\eta)^\top,\;
   \nu + T\big)$.
2. Draw $\boldsymbol\eta$ with the $\boldsymbol\mu_t$ integrated out, from
   $\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\eta_T, \boldsymbol\Phi_T)$ with $\boldsymbol\Phi_T =
   \big[\boldsymbol\Phi^{-1} + \sum_t (\boldsymbol\Omega +
   \boldsymbol\Sigma_t)^{-1}\big]^{-1}$ and $\boldsymbol\eta_T =
   \boldsymbol\Phi_T\big[\boldsymbol\Phi^{-1}\boldsymbol\eta_0 + \sum_t
   (\boldsymbol\Omega + \boldsymbol\Sigma_t)^{-1}\mathbf z_t\big]$.
3. Draw each $\boldsymbol\mu_t$ from @eq-oec-blup.

The Student-t sampler adds a latent scale per test, $d_t \sim \chi^2(\gamma)$ with
$\boldsymbol\mu_t \mid d_t \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\eta, (\gamma/d_t)\,
\boldsymbol\Omega)$, which restores conjugacy; every $\boldsymbol\Omega$ above is
rescaled by $\gamma/d_t$, the scales are drawn from a gamma distribution, and
$\gamma$ gets a Metropolis step. The DPM sampler reassigns each test to a cluster
with probability proportional to the cluster's size times the posterior predictive
density of $\boldsymbol\mu_t$ under that cluster (a multivariate Student-t), or to
a new cluster with probability proportional to $\alpha_0$ times the prior
predictive density [@neal2000dpm, algorithm 3], and then runs the Gaussian blocks
within each cluster. The concentration parameter is updated by the
data-augmentation step of @escobar1995density.

The authors recommend weakly informative hyperpriors: $\boldsymbol\eta_0 = \mathbf
0$ (the average change does nothing), a diffuse $\boldsymbol\Phi$, a small $\nu$,
a prior on $\gamma$ that covers roughly 5 to 10 degrees of freedom, and $\alpha_0$
between 0.5 and 2. Cost scales linearly in the number of tests for the Gaussian and
Student-t models, as $T \log T$ for the DPM, and as $p^3$ in the number of metrics,
so the practical range is around ten metrics or fewer. On 190 tests with five
metrics and 30,000 draws, the authors report 1.35 minutes for the Gaussian model
with $\boldsymbol\eta$ fixed at zero, 2.45 for the Gaussian, 4.73 for the
Student-t, and 142.53 for the DPM. Tests with several treatment arms are handled by
stacking the arms' effect vectors and using their joint covariance.

### What the paper finds {#sec-causal-oec-findings}

**Simulation.** The authors fit the DPM to the Zillow archive, draw 100 synthetic
archives from its posterior predictive distribution (transformed so that nothing
confidential survives), and run six methods on each: the naive estimator (N), a
Gaussian model with the prior mean fixed at zero (G-0), the Gaussian (G), the
Student-t (T), the DPM, and a metaregression (MR) in which each test's cluster is
known, as it would be if tests were tagged by type. @tbl-oec-paper-sim reproduces
their headline table.

| Metric | N | G-0 | G | T | DPM | MR |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Correct decision rate | 0.81 | 0.84 | 0.87 | 0.87 | 0.91 | 0.93 |
| Regret | 0.05 | 0.03 | 0.02 | 0.02 | 0.01 | 0.01 |
| Overestimation among shipped variants | 0.48 | 0.01 | 0.01 | 0.02 | −0.01 | −0.01 |
| Mean absolute error | 1.01 | 0.16 | 0.15 | 0.15 | 0.11 | 0.09 |
| Average 95% interval length | 4.95 | 0.98 | 0.94 | 0.98 | 0.56 | 0.49 |
| 95% interval coverage | 0.95 | 0.97 | 0.97 | 0.98 | 0.97 | 0.97 |

: Simulation results reported by @huch2026oec (their Table 1), averaged over 100 synthetic archives. A variant is "shipped" when its estimated OEC is positive; regret is the OEC lost relative to the better arm. {#tbl-oec-paper-sim}

Three patterns are visible. Every meta-analytic method beats the naive one on every
criterion, and the largest single step is from N to G-0: most of the gain comes
from having a prior at all. The naive method overstates the value of what it ships
by 0.48, about half its own mean absolute error, while the meta-analytic methods
are within 0.02 of zero. And the intervals from the meta-analytic methods are less
than a fifth as long yet cover slightly *more* than 95%, the mild overcoverage
being the price of hyperpriors that were deliberately not tuned to the truth. The
DPM and MR cut wrong decisions by more than half relative to the naive method (from
19% to 9% and 7%).

**The Zillow archive.** The application uses 190 tests run during part of 2022 to
2024: email campaigns, site design changes, new features, personalization models.
The KPIs are the rescaled dollar impact per customer on two undisclosed lines of
business, the OEC is their sum, and three undisclosed short-term metrics serve as
proxies. Ground truth is unavailable, so the authors split each test's customers in
half, fit every method on one half, and score its predictions against the naive
estimate from the other half, which is noisy but unbiased under minimal
assumptions.

On that test the meta-analytic methods predict the held-out estimate better than
the naive method in 69% to 73% of tests. The DPM's log absolute error is lower by
0.29, about 25% less absolute error; the Student-t is close behind at 0.27, and the
two Gaussian models are at 0.21 to 0.22. All five methods have prediction-interval
coverage between 0.94 and 0.96, and the DPM's median interval is about a quarter
shorter than the naive one (1.55 against 2.06). These gains are smaller than in the
simulation because the yardstick is itself a noisy half-sample estimate. The
sharpest diagnostic is the rank correlation between a method's prediction and its
own prediction error. For the naive method it is −0.59: the bigger the claimed
win, the bigger the subsequent disappointment. For the DPM it is −0.14. A second
set of hyperpriors that changes almost every setting leaves the ordering of the
methods intact.

Fitted to the full data, the DPM gives the surrogacy measures in
@tbl-oec-paper-surrogacy.

| Measure | KPI 1 | KPI 2 | OEC (sum) |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| $R^2$ | 0.52 (0.18–0.90) | 0.78 (0.42–0.98) | 0.46 (0.13–0.81) |
| TVR | 0.16 (0.08–0.24) | 0.10 (0.04–0.19) | 0.15 (0.08–0.24) |
| PVR | 0.18 (0.10–0.27) | 0.13 (0.06–0.22) | 0.17 (0.10–0.26) |
| SVR | 0.91 (0.82–0.97) | 0.88 (0.79–0.95) | 0.93 (0.84–0.97) |

: Aggregate surrogacy measures for the Zillow archive reported by @huch2026oec (their Table 5): posterior means with 95% credible intervals, averaged over 190 tests. {#tbl-oec-paper-surrogacy}

The table deserves a careful reading, because it qualifies the paper's own framing.
A TVR of 0.15 means the posterior standard deviation of the OEC is about 60% smaller
than the naive standard error, the equivalent of a test six to ten times larger.
But the decomposition shows that almost all of that comes from the PVR: shrinking
the noisy KPI estimates toward the archive's distribution does the work, and the
proxies add a further 7% to 12% reduction in variance on top. The proxies are
moderately strong surrogates ($R^2$ around 0.5) and still contribute little, since
the prior has already removed most of the noise they could have removed. In this
archive the method earns its keep as a shrinkage estimator first and as a
surrogate model second. Where the proxies become indispensable is the early
readout of @eq-oec-missing, when the KPI has not been observed at all.

The DPM finds a posterior mean of 7.2 clusters (95% interval 4 to 12), and the
clusters are interpretable after the fact: one is dominated by tests of rental
search, another contains only mobile tests. The authors suggest using such
clusters to discover the metadata a metaregression should condition on. Posterior
predictive checks for dependence between the effects and their sampling variances
give a smallest p-value of 0.05 across ten comparisons, little evidence against
exchangeability.

### Replication {#sec-causal-oec-replication}

The Zillow data are confidential, and the authors' replication package (synthetic
archives and Python code) sits behind a registration form on the INFORMS site, so
it was not used here. What follows is an independent implementation in R, written
from the paper's Section 4 and Appendix B, in `replication/oec-meta/` of the book's
repository. It reproduces the estimators and the design of the simulation study,
not the paper's numbers, because the data-generating process is ours.

The Gaussian model is short enough to run inline. The chunk below simulates an
archive of 190 tests with one noisy KPI and two precise proxies, learns
$(\boldsymbol\eta, \boldsymbol\Omega)$ by the EM algorithm (an empirical-Bayes
shortcut that plugs in point estimates where the paper integrates over a
posterior), and compares three estimates of each test's long-run effect: the naive
one, the BLUP of @eq-oec-blup, and the early readout of @eq-oec-missing that never
sees the KPI.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(47)

# --- An archive of 190 past A/B tests ----------------------------------------
# Three metrics per test: y = effect on six-month revenue per customer (the KPI),
# x1 = effect on click-through, x2 = effect on form-fill rate (the proxies).
n_tests <- 190; p <- 3
eta   <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.08)                        # average true effect
sd_mu <- c(0.30, 0.40, 0.35)
R_mu  <- matrix(c(1, .7, .6,  .7, 1, .5,  .6, .5, 1), p, p)
Omega <- diag(sd_mu) %*% R_mu %*% diag(sd_mu)       # cross-test covariance of true effects
mu    <- sweep(matrix(rnorm(n_tests * p), n_tests) %*% chol(Omega), 2, eta, "+")

# Sampling noise: the KPI is rare and slow, so it is far noisier than the proxies.
size  <- rlnorm(n_tests, 0, 0.6)                    # tests differ in sample size
C_err <- matrix(c(1, .3, .3,  .3, 1, .2,  .3, .2, 1), p, p)
Sigma <- lapply(size, function(h) { s <- c(0.50, 0.12, 0.15) / sqrt(h)
                                    diag(s) %*% C_err %*% diag(s) })
z <- t(sapply(seq_len(n_tests), function(t)
  mu[t, ] + drop(rnorm(p) %*% chol(Sigma[[t]]))))

# --- The BLUP: combine the prior N(eta, Omega) with z_t ~ N(mu_t, Sigma_t) -----
# `seen` marks the metrics already observed for this test.
blup <- function(z_t, S_t, eta, Omega, seen = rep(TRUE, length(z_t))) {
  prec <- matrix(0, length(z_t), length(z_t))
  prec[seen, seen] <- solve(S_t[seen, seen])
  V <- solve(solve(Omega) + prec)
  list(mean = drop(V %*% (solve(Omega, eta) + prec %*% replace(z_t, !seen, 0))),
       cov = V)
}

# --- Learn (eta, Omega) from the archive by EM (empirical Bayes) --------------
eta_hat <- colMeans(z); Omega_hat <- cov(z)
for (iter in 1:500) {
  post <- lapply(seq_len(n_tests), function(t)
    blup(z[t, ], Sigma[[t]], eta_hat, Omega_hat))
  m <- t(sapply(post, `[[`, "mean"))
  eta_hat <- colMeans(m)
  Omega_hat <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(seq_len(n_tests), function(t)
    post[[t]]$cov + tcrossprod(m[t, ] - eta_hat))) / n_tests
}

# --- Three estimates of each test's OEC (the true KPI effect) ------------------
full  <- lapply(seq_len(n_tests), function(t)
  blup(z[t, ], Sigma[[t]], eta_hat, Omega_hat))
early <- lapply(seq_len(n_tests), function(t)
  blup(z[t, ], Sigma[[t]], eta_hat, Omega_hat, seen = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)))
est <- data.frame(
  naive = z[, 1], se_naive = sqrt(sapply(Sigma, `[`, 1, 1)),
  meta  = sapply(full,  function(b) b$mean[1]),
  se_meta  = sqrt(sapply(full,  function(b) b$cov[1, 1])),
  early = sapply(early, function(b) b$mean[1]),
  se_early = sqrt(sapply(early, function(b) b$cov[1, 1])))
truth <- mu[, 1]

score <- function(e, se) {
  ship <- e > 0
  c("Correct decision rate"             = mean(ship == (truth > 0)),
    "Overestimation, shipped variants"  = mean((e - truth)[ship]),
    "Mean absolute error"               = mean(abs(e - truth)),
    "Mean 95% interval length"          = mean(2 * 1.96 * se),
    "95% interval coverage"             = mean(abs(e - truth) <= 1.96 * se))
}
oec_demo <- cbind("Naive (KPI only)"              = score(est$naive, est$se_naive),
                  "Meta-analytic (KPI + proxies)" = score(est$meta,  est$se_meta),
                  "Early readout (proxies only)"  = score(est$early, est$se_early))

# --- Surrogacy diagnostics at the median-sized test ----------------------------
S_med <- Sigma[[which.min(abs(size - median(size)))]]
v0 <- S_med[1, 1]
vz <- blup(z[1, ], S_med, eta_hat, Omega_hat)$cov[1, 1]
vy <- 1 / (1 / Omega_hat[1, 1] + 1 / v0)
oec_diag <- c(R2  = drop(Omega_hat[1, 2:3] %*%
                           solve(Omega_hat[2:3, 2:3], Omega_hat[2:3, 1])) / Omega_hat[1, 1],
              TVR = vz / v0, PVR = vy / v0, SVR = vz / vy)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2.2, 1))
lim <- range(est$naive)
plot(truth, est$naive, pch = 16, cex = .6, col = "grey55", ylim = lim,
     xlab = "True effect on the KPI", ylab = "Estimate",
     main = "Naive: one test at a time")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
plot(truth, est$meta, pch = 16, cex = .6, col = "steelblue4", ylim = lim,
     xlab = "True effect on the KPI", ylab = "Estimate",
     main = "Meta-analytic posterior mean")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
par(op)
```

0.31, against a mean absolute error of

archive a KPI estimate with a standard error near 0.5 adds little to two precise
proxies and a prior. The diagnostics say the same thing in the paper's vocabulary.
At the median-sized test the estimated $R^2$ of the proxies is
0.40 (the true value in the simulation is 0.57, and
the gap is a reminder that $\boldsymbol\Omega$ is itself estimated from noisy
tests), the total variance ratio is 0.27, and it
factors into a prior variance ratio of 0.35 and a
surrogacy variance ratio of 0.77. The plug-in
intervals ignore the uncertainty in $(\hat{\boldsymbol\eta},
\hat{\boldsymbol\Omega})$, which is one reason to prefer the fully Bayesian version
when the archive is small.

The fully Bayesian samplers are in `oec_samplers.R`: `gibbs_re()` fits the Gaussian,
Gaussian-0, and Student-t models, `gibbs_dpm()` fits the DPM and (given known
