```{.r .cell-code}
# Meta-analytic overall evaluation criteria (OEC) for A/B tests.
#
# R implementation of the estimators in
#   Huch, Nail, Melconian, Vongsathorn & Feinberg (2026), "Overall Evaluation
#   Criteria for A/B Tests: A Meta-Analytic Approach", Marketing Science,
#   doi:10.1287/mksc.2025.0164
# written from the paper's Section 4 and Appendix B. The authors' own code is
# Python; this is an independent reimplementation in base R (no packages).
#
# Data layout used throughout
#   z      T x p matrix of estimated treatment effects, one row per A/B test.
#          Columns 1..r are the KPIs (y), columns r+1..p the proxies (x).
#   Sigma  p x p x T array; Sigma[, , t] is the sampling covariance of z[t, ].
#   obs    optional T x p logical matrix; FALSE marks a metric not yet observed
#          for that test (paper eq. 6). Missing entries of z may hold anything.
#
# Every sampler returns posterior draws of mu_t (n_keep x T x p) so that any
# OEC f(mu_y) can be evaluated draw by draw.

# ---- small linear-algebra helpers -------------------------------------------

rmvn <- function(mean, cov) {
  drop(mean + crossprod(chol(cov), rnorm(length(mean))))
}

# Omega ~ inverse-Wishart(Psi, nu)  <=>  Omega^{-1} ~ Wishart(Psi^{-1}, nu)
riwish <- function(nu, Psi) {
  chol2inv(chol(rWishart(1, nu, chol2inv(chol(Psi)))[, , 1]))
}

# A' (A M A')^{-1} A for the selection matrix A that keeps the observed metrics:
# the precision contributed by a partially observed test (paper eq. 6, B.2).
prec_obs <- function(M, o) {
  out <- matrix(0, nrow(M), ncol(M))
  if (any(o)) out[o, o] <- chol2inv(chol(M[o, o, drop = FALSE]))
  out
}

# log density of a multivariate Student-t with location m, scale matrix S, df
ldmvt <- function(x, m, S, df) {
  p <- length(x)
  R <- chol(S)
  q <- sum(backsolve(R, x - m, transpose = TRUE)^2)
  lgamma((df + p) / 2) - lgamma(df / 2) - p / 2 * log(df * pi) -
    sum(log(diag(R))) - (df + p) / 2 * log1p(q / df)
}

# ---- the naive single-test benchmark (paper eq. 1-2) ------------------------

oec_naive <- function(z, Sigma, r) {
  u <- c(rep(1, r), rep(0, ncol(z) - r))
  est <- drop(z %*% u)
  se <- sqrt(apply(Sigma, 3, function(S) drop(t(u) %*% S %*% u)))
  data.frame(est = est, se = se, lo = est - qnorm(.975) * se,
             hi = est + qnorm(.975) * se)
}

# ---- conditional draw of every mu_t given its prior N(eta_t, Omega_t) -------
# eta: T x p matrix of prior means; Omega: list or array of prior covariances
# indexed by `idx` (length T). Implements eq. (5b) / (6).

draw_mu <- function(z, Sigma, obs, eta, Omega_inv, idx, scale = NULL) {
  T <- nrow(z); p <- ncol(z)
  mu <- matrix(0, T, p)
  for (t in seq_len(T)) {
    Oi <- Omega_inv[, , idx[t]]
    if (!is.null(scale)) Oi <- Oi / scale[t]          # prior cov = scale * Omega
    o <- obs[t, ]
    Si <- prec_obs(Sigma[, , t], o)
    V <- chol2inv(chol(Oi + Si))
    zt <- z[t, ]; zt[!o] <- 0
    m <- V %*% (Oi %*% eta[t, ] + Si %*% zt)
    mu[t, ] <- rmvn(drop(m), V)
  }
  mu
}

# collapsed draw of a location eta given z_t ~ N(eta, Omega_t + Sigma_t), t in S
# with prior N(m0, V0)  (paper eq. B.2 and B.5)
draw_eta <- function(z, Sigma, obs, S, Omega, m0, V0_inv, scale = NULL) {
  P <- V0_inv
  b <- V0_inv %*% m0
  for (t in S) {
    o <- obs[t, ]
    Om <- if (is.null(scale)) Omega else Omega * scale[t]
    W <- prec_obs(Om + Sigma[, , t], o)
    zt <- z[t, ]; zt[!o] <- 0
    P <- P + W
    b <- b + W %*% zt
  }
  V <- chol2inv(chol(P))
  rmvn(drop(V %*% b), V)
}

# ---- Gaussian and Student-t random-effects models (Appendix B.1, B.2) -------
#   mu_t ~ N(eta, Omega)                      model = "gaussian"
#   mu_t ~ t(eta, Omega, gamma)               model = "t"
#   fix_eta = TRUE pins eta at eta0: the paper's "Gaussian-0" variant.
# Priors: eta ~ N(eta0, Phi), Omega ~ IW(Psi, nu), log(gamma) ~ N(lg_mean, lg_sd).

gibbs_re <- function(z, Sigma, n_iter = 3000, burn = 1000, model = "gaussian",
                     fix_eta = FALSE, obs = NULL,
                     eta0 = rep(0, ncol(z)), Phi = diag(ncol(z)),
                     Psi = 8 * diag(ncol(z)), nu = 8,
                     lg_mean = 2, lg_sd = 1, lg_step = 0.4) {
  T <- nrow(z); p <- ncol(z)
  if (is.null(obs)) obs <- matrix(TRUE, T, p)
  Phi_inv <- chol2inv(chol(Phi))
  mu <- z; mu[!obs] <- 0
  eta <- if (fix_eta) eta0 else colMeans(mu)
  gam <- exp(lg_mean); d <- rep(gam, T)
  keep <- n_iter - burn
  out <- list(mu = array(0, c(keep, T, p)), eta = matrix(0, keep, p),
              Omega = array(0, c(keep, p, p)), gamma = numeric(keep))
  for (it in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    E <- sweep(mu, 2, eta)
    w <- if (model == "t") d / gam else rep(1, T)
    # Omega | mu, eta (, d)                                      eq. (B.1)
    Omega <- riwish(nu + T, Psi + crossprod(E * sqrt(w)))
    Omega_inv <- chol2inv(chol(Omega))
    if (model == "t") {
      q <- rowSums((E %*% Omega_inv) * E)
      # gamma | mu, eta, Omega with d integrated out: random-walk MH on log gamma
      ll <- function(g) sum(lgamma((g + p) / 2) - lgamma(g / 2) -
                              p / 2 * log(g) - (g + p) / 2 * log1p(q / g))
      lg <- log(gam); lg_new <- lg + rnorm(1, 0, lg_step)
      a <- ll(exp(lg_new)) + dnorm(lg_new, lg_mean, lg_sd, log = TRUE) -
        ll(gam) - dnorm(lg, lg_mean, lg_sd, log = TRUE)
      if (log(runif(1)) < a) gam <- exp(lg_new)
      # d_t | gamma, mu_t, eta, Omega
      d <- rgamma(T, (gam + p) / 2, rate = (1 + q / gam) / 2)
    }
    sc <- if (model == "t") gam / d else NULL
    # eta | Omega, z with mu integrated out                       eq. (B.2)
    if (!fix_eta)
      eta <- draw_eta(z, Sigma, obs, seq_len(T), Omega, eta0, Phi_inv, sc)
    # mu_t | eta, Omega, z_t                                      eq. (5)
    mu <- draw_mu(z, Sigma, obs, matrix(eta, T, p, byrow = TRUE),
                  array(Omega_inv, c(p, p, 1)), rep(1, T), sc)
    if (it > burn) {
      k <- it - burn
      out$mu[k, , ] <- mu; out$eta[k, ] <- eta
      out$Omega[k, , ] <- Omega; out$gamma[k] <- gam
    }
  }
  out
}

# ---- Dirichlet process mixture of Gaussians (Appendix B.3) ------------------
#   mu_t | c_t ~ N(eta_{c_t}, Omega_{c_t}),  (eta_k, Omega_k) ~ NIW(eta0, phi, Psi, nu)
# Collapsed sampler (Neal 2000, algorithm 3) for the cluster labels, then the
# paper's blocked updates for Omega_k, eta_k and mu_t.
#
# Hyperpriors: alpha0 ~ Gamma(a_alpha, b_alpha)  (Escobar & West 1995 update),
#   eta0 ~ N(0, I), phi ~ Gamma(1, 1), and Psi ~ Wishart(Psi_V, Psi_df).
# The paper puts an inverse-Wishart hyperprior on Psi, which needs a Metropolis
# step; a Wishart hyperprior with the same prior mean is conditionally conjugate
# and is what is used here. nu is fixed, as in the paper.
#
# fixed_c: supply known group labels to get the paper's "metaregression" (MR)
# variant, in which cluster membership is observed rather than inferred.

gibbs_dpm <- function(z, Sigma, n_iter = 3000, burn = 1000, obs = NULL,
                      fixed_c = NULL, nu = 10, a_alpha = 4, b_alpha = 4,
                      Psi_V = diag(ncol(z)) / 2, Psi_df = 8, K_init = 5,
                      keep_Omega = FALSE) {
  T <- nrow(z); p <- ncol(z)
  if (is.null(obs)) obs <- matrix(TRUE, T, p)
  mu <- z; mu[!obs] <- 0
  cl <- if (!is.null(fixed_c)) as.integer(factor(fixed_c)) else
    as.integer(kmeans(mu, K_init)$cluster)
  eta0 <- rep(0, p); phi <- 1; alpha0 <- a_alpha / b_alpha
  Psi <- Psi_V * Psi_df
  keep <- n_iter - burn
  out <- list(mu = array(0, c(keep, T, p)), cl = matrix(0L, keep, T),
              K = integer(keep), alpha0 = numeric(keep))
  if (keep_Omega) out$Om_t <- array(0, c(keep, T, p, p))

  niw_post <- function(n, s, SS) {            # paper eq. (B.4)
    if (n == 0) return(list(nu = nu, phi = phi, eta = eta0, Psi = Psi))
    mbar <- s / n
    S <- SS - n * tcrossprod(mbar)
    list(nu = nu + n, phi = phi + n, eta = (phi * eta0 + s) / (phi + n),
         Psi = Psi + S + phi * n / (phi + n) * tcrossprod(mbar - eta0))
  }
  lpred <- function(x, n, s, SS) {            # paper eq. (B.3)
    h <- niw_post(n, s, SS)
    df <- h$nu - p + 1
    ldmvt(x, h$eta, (1 + 1 / h$phi) * h$Psi / df, df)
  }

  for (it in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    K <- max(cl)
    n <- tabulate(cl, K)
    s <- rowsum(mu, cl, reorder = TRUE)                       # K x p
    SS <- array(0, c(p, p, K))
    for (k in seq_len(K)) SS[, , k] <- crossprod(mu[cl == k, , drop = FALSE])

    if (is.null(fixed_c)) {
      for (t in seq_len(T)) {
        k0 <- cl[t]; x <- mu[t, ]; xx <- tcrossprod(x)
        n[k0] <- n[k0] - 1; s[k0, ] <- s[k0, ] - x; SS[, , k0] <- SS[, , k0] - xx
        if (n[k0] == 0) {                     # drop the emptied cluster
          n <- n[-k0]; s <- s[-k0, , drop = FALSE]; SS <- SS[, , -k0, drop = FALSE]
          cl[cl > k0] <- cl[cl > k0] - 1L; K <- K - 1L
        }
        lp <- numeric(K + 1)
        for (k in seq_len(K)) lp[k] <- log(n[k]) + lpred(x, n[k], s[k, ], SS[, , k])
        lp[K + 1] <- log(alpha0) + lpred(x, 0, 0, 0)
        k1 <- sample.int(K + 1, 1, prob = exp(lp - max(lp)))
        if (k1 > K) {
          K <- K + 1L; n <- c(n, 0); s <- rbind(s, 0)
          SS <- array(c(SS, rep(0, p * p)), c(p, p, K))
        }
        cl[t] <- k1
        n[k1] <- n[k1] + 1; s[k1, ] <- s[k1, ] + x; SS[, , k1] <- SS[, , k1] + xx
      }
    }

    # Omega_k | mu, c  then  eta_k | Omega_k, z (mu integrated out)   eq. (B.5)
    Omega <- array(0, c(p, p, K)); Omega_inv <- Omega; eta <- matrix(0, K, p)
    for (k in seq_len(K)) {
      h <- niw_post(n[k], s[k, ], SS[, , k])
      Omega[, , k] <- riwish(h$nu, h$Psi)
      Omega_inv[, , k] <- chol2inv(chol(Omega[, , k]))
      eta[k, ] <- draw_eta(z, Sigma, obs, which(cl == k), Omega[, , k],
                           eta0, phi * Omega_inv[, , k])
    }
    # mu_t | eta_{c_t}, Omega_{c_t}, z_t                              eq. (5)
    mu <- draw_mu(z, Sigma, obs, eta[cl, , drop = FALSE], Omega_inv, cl)

    # hyperparameters
    if (is.null(fixed_c)) {
      kap <- rbeta(1, alpha0 + 1, T)
      odds <- (a_alpha + K - 1) / (T * (b_alpha - log(kap)))
      alpha0 <- rgamma(1, a_alpha + K - (runif(1) > odds / (1 + odds)),
                       rate = b_alpha - log(kap))
    }
    P <- diag(p); b <- rep(0, p); qsum <- 0; Oi_sum <- matrix(0, p, p)
    for (k in seq_len(K)) {
      P <- P + phi * Omega_inv[, , k]
      b <- b + phi * Omega_inv[, , k] %*% eta[k, ]
      Oi_sum <- Oi_sum + Omega_inv[, , k]
    }
    V <- chol2inv(chol(P)); eta0 <- rmvn(drop(V %*% b), V)
    for (k in seq_len(K)) {
      e <- eta[k, ] - eta0
      qsum <- qsum + drop(t(e) %*% Omega_inv[, , k] %*% e)
    }
    phi <- rgamma(1, 1 + K * p / 2, rate = 1 + qsum / 2)
    Psi <- rWishart(1, Psi_df + K * nu,
                    chol2inv(chol(chol2inv(chol(Psi_V)) + Oi_sum)))[, , 1]

    if (it > burn) {
      k <- it - burn
      out$mu[k, , ] <- mu; out$cl[k, ] <- cl; out$K[k] <- K
      out$alpha0[k] <- alpha0
      if (keep_Omega) for (t in seq_len(T)) out$Om_t[k, t, , ] <- Omega[, , cl[t]]
    }
  }
  out
}

# Surrogacy measures of Section 4.1 for one prior covariance Omega and one
# test's sampling covariance Sigma_t, for the summed OEC over the first r metrics:
#   R2  share of prior OEC variance explained by the proxies          eq. (7)
#   TVR posterior variance / naive variance  (= PVR * SVR)
#   PVR variance ratio from the prior on the KPIs alone (proxies discarded)
#   SVR further ratio from adding the proxies
surrogacy <- function(Omega, Sigma_t, r) {
  p <- nrow(Omega); iy <- seq_len(r); ix <- (r + 1):p
  one <- rep(1, r); u <- c(one, rep(0, p - r))
  R2 <- drop(t(one) %*% Omega[iy, ix] %*% solve(Omega[ix, ix], Omega[ix, iy]) %*% one) /
    drop(t(one) %*% Omega[iy, iy] %*% one)
  v0 <- drop(t(u) %*% Sigma_t %*% u)
  vz <- drop(t(u) %*% solve(solve(Omega) + solve(Sigma_t)) %*% u)
  vy <- drop(t(one) %*% solve(solve(Omega[iy, iy]) + solve(Sigma_t[iy, iy])) %*% one)
  c(R2 = R2, TVR = vz / v0, PVR = vy / v0, SVR = vz / vy)
}
```

### Using the method {#sec-causal-oec-practice}

For a team that wants to adopt this, the paper implies a sequence.

1. Build the archive. Store $(\mathbf z_t, \boldsymbol\Sigma_t)$ for every
   test, with the full covariance matrix, fixed metric definitions, and fixed
   measurement windows. Exclude tests that fail quality checks such as
   sample-ratio mismatch.
2. Define the OEC in business terms. Choose the KPIs and the function $f$ so
   that the target is long-run value, and resist redefining it when a proxy is
   convenient. The proxies enter through the model, not through the definition.
3. Start with the Gaussian model. It runs in minutes, its posterior mean is a
   linear rule that can be explained to a product manager, and in both the paper's
   results and ours it captures most of the gain over the naive method.
4. **Check exchangeability.** Test for dependence between estimated effects and
   test metadata, including sampling variances. If the DPM finds clusters that line
   up with something observable, condition on it.
5. **Read the diagnostics before trusting the proxies.** A low $R^2$ or an SVR near
   one says the proxies add little once the KPI is observed, and that early
   readouts will be weak.
6. **Refit on a schedule and validate.** Refit as tests mature, score early
   readouts against mature estimates, and track the rank correlation between
   predictions and errors as a running check on regression to the mean.

Three limits should be kept in view. The framework estimates the long-run effect
of the treatment as it was run, a short exposure whose consequences are followed
for months; the effect of leaving a feature on permanently is a different
estimand and needs a forecasting model. Exchangeability is an assumption about
the firm's process for generating ideas, and it can break when that process
changes, for instance when a team shifts from incremental tweaks to redesigns.
And the posterior for any one test depends on every other test in the archive, so
an archive curated toward successes will produce a prior that is too optimistic.

The method belongs to a family that this book meets in two other places. Predicted
incrementality by experimentation (@sec-adv-pie) also treats a library of
experiments as training data, but it predicts the effect of campaigns that had no
control group at all, from features of the treated group, with a supervised
learner and no measurement model. Matrix completion across overlapping experiments
(@sec-adv-overlap) recovers outcomes for treatment combinations that were never
run. The meta-analytic OEC is the member of the family built for the most common
situation in a product organization: the test was run, the short-run metrics are
in, and the decision cannot wait for the metric that matters.

## Difference-in-Differences {#sec-causal-did}

When randomization is impossible—a competitor enters a market, a regulator changes
a privacy rule, a firm rolls a price change out to some regions before others—the
analyst exploits *timing*. **Difference-in-differences** compares the change in
outcomes for a treated group, before versus after the intervention, against the
contemporaneous change for an untreated control group. Differencing over time
removes any fixed differences between the groups; differencing across groups
removes any common time trend. What remains, under one key assumption, is the
treatment effect. @fig-ci-did-logic traces the two subtractions.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-ci-did-logic
%%| fig-cap: "The difference-in-differences logic. Each within-group change over time removes that group's fixed level; the difference of the two changes removes the common time trend. What remains is the ATT, provided the untreated trends are parallel."
flowchart LR
  subgraph TG["Treated group"]
    TP["Mean outcome,<br/>pre-period"] --> TQ["Mean outcome,<br/>post-period"]
  end
  subgraph CG["Control group"]
    CP["Mean outcome,<br/>pre-period"] --> CQ["Mean outcome,<br/>post-period"]
  end
  TP --> DT["First difference, treated:<br/>fixed group differences drop out"]
  TQ --> DT
  CP --> DC["First difference, control:<br/>fixed group differences drop out"]
  CQ --> DC
  DT --> DD["Difference of differences:<br/>common time trend drops out;<br/>equals the ATT under parallel trends"]
  DC --> DD
```

Formally, with two periods (pre, post) and two groups (treated $T$, control $C$),
the DiD estimator is the difference of differences in group means,

$$
\hat\tau_{\text{DiD}}
= \big(\bar Y_{T,\text{post}} - \bar Y_{T,\text{pre}}\big)
- \big(\bar Y_{C,\text{post}} - \bar Y_{C,\text{pre}}\big).
$$ {#eq-47-did}

In panel-regression form, with unit fixed effects $\alpha_i$, time fixed effects
$\gamma_t$, and a treatment indicator $D_{it}$ equal to one for treated units in
post-treatment periods,

$$
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \tau\,D_{it} + \varepsilon_{it},
$$ {#eq-twfe}

and $\hat\tau$ is the DiD (two-way fixed-effects) estimator of the ATT.

**Identifying assumption: parallel trends.** DiD is unbiased for the ATT if, *absent
treatment*, the treated and control groups would have followed the same trajectory:

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}(0) - Y_{i,\text{pre}}(0) \mid T]
= \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}(0) - Y_{i,\text{pre}}(0) \mid C].
$$ {#eq-parallel-trends}

The groups may differ in *levels*—that is differenced away—but their untreated
*trends* must coincide. This assumption is fundamentally untestable, because the
treated group's untreated post-period trend is the missing counterfactual. What
*is* testable is its observable implication: if trends are parallel after
treatment, they were typically parallel before. A **pre-trends** (event-study)
check estimates leads and lags of the treatment and asks whether the pre-treatment
leads are jointly zero.

**What breaks identification.** Parallel trends fails whenever something other than
the treatment moves the groups differently over the window—a localized demand
shock, mean reversion when treatment is assigned to units with unusually low recent
outcomes (Ashenfelter's dip), or anticipation effects. A subtler hazard has emerged
in **staggered adoption**, where units are treated at different times: the standard
two-way fixed-effects estimator in @eq-twfe implicitly uses already-treated units
as controls for later-treated ones, and when effects vary over time this
"forbidden comparison" can produce a weighted average with *negative weights* and a
biased—even wrong-signed—estimate. Modern heterogeneity-robust estimators address
this, and a careful analyst reports both the two-way fixed-effects number and a
robust alternative.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(47)

# Panel: 60 markets x 12 months. Treatment (a price cut) hits half the markets
# in month 7. The control group is constructed to satisfy parallel trends.
n_markets <- 60; n_months <- 12; treat_month <- 7; true_att <- 1.5
markets <- 1:n_markets
treated <- markets %in% sample(markets, n_markets / 2)

panel <- expand.grid(market = markets, month = 1:n_months)
panel$treated <- treated[panel$market]
market_fe <- rnorm(n_markets, 10, 2)[panel$market]   # level differences (ok)
time_fe   <- 0.20 * panel$month                       # common trend (ok)
post      <- panel$month >= treat_month
panel$D   <- as.integer(panel$treated & post)
panel$sales <- market_fe + time_fe + true_att * panel$D +
               rnorm(nrow(panel), 0, 0.8)

# DiD via two-way fixed effects (unit + time dummies).
fit <- lm(sales ~ factor(market) + factor(month) + D, data = panel)
att_hat <- coef(fit)["D"]
ci <- confint(fit)["D", ]
cat(sprintf("True ATT:        %.3f\n", true_att))
#> True ATT:        1.500
cat(sprintf("DiD estimate:    %.3f  [%.3f, %.3f]\n", att_hat, ci[1], ci[2]))
#> DiD estimate:    1.662  [1.437, 1.886]
```
:::


DiD is the workhorse of *advertising-spillover* and *pricing* studies in marketing,
precisely because firms so often roll changes out geographically and at staggered
times—exactly the structure DiD exploits, and exactly the structure that demands
the heterogeneity-robust care just described.

A platform feature rolled out product by product shows what that care looks like when
the platform, not the researcher, chooses the timing. @wang2026reviewsummaries estimate
how Amazon's AI-generated review summaries affect review volume
(@sec-online-ai-summaries), and their online appendix covers four checks that any
staggered design of this kind should report. (1) *Robust estimator next to TWFE.* The
two-way estimate on log(reviews + 1) is 0.071 without controls and 0.060 with them. The
Callaway–Sant'Anna estimate [@callaway2021did] is 0.039 and 0.052. Both robust estimates
are smaller, which is the kind of gap the forbidden-comparison critique
[@goodmanbacon2021differencdifferenc] says can open, and both remain clearly positive. (2) *Model the timing.* A Cox hazard
model of when each product received its summary includes the outcome's five weekly
lags. None of them predicts adoption, so the platform did not visibly target products
whose reviews were already rising. Price and product tenure do predict adoption, which
is why they belong among the controls. (3) *Use a second control population.* The same
products on a storefront or retailer without the feature (Amazon UK, Walmart) give a
comparison that does not depend on not-yet-treated products. (4) *Check the transform.*
With many zero-review weeks, log(y + 1) estimates depend on the outcome's units. The
authors also report Poisson and untransformed-count estimates (about 0.33 more reviews
per product-week), which is the defensible way to state the magnitude.

A government program rolled out place by place gives a third pattern, in which every
unit in the sample is eventually treated. @agarwal2026road study whether India's rural
road program drew households into the stock market (@sec-sw-emb-roads), and the
working-paper version [@agarwal2022roadwp] keeps only the 4,154 postal codes that
received a first road during the sample window. Dropping never-connected places removes
the comparison most exposed to selection, since places that never get a road differ
from those that do. Identification then rests on timing alone, and that has three
consequences worth stating in any paper built this way. (1) *The event study loses a
degree of freedom.* Without a never-treated group, unit and calendar-time fixed effects
absorb a linear trend in time since treatment, so two event-time coefficients have to
be omitted instead of one. The authors drop the year before completion and the earliest
lead. (2) *The pre-trend test is weaker than it looks.* With two leads normalized to
zero, the remaining leads can only reveal departures from a linear pre-trend. The
working paper says so, and reports a joint test of the pre-period coefficients
($p = 0.58$). (3) *Controls run out.* A group-time estimator [@callaway2021did] must use
not-yet-treated units as controls, and the last cohort to be treated has none, so
late-period effects are either not identified or rest on few comparison units. The
working paper adds a placebo that fits this design well: reassign completion dates at
random, 500 times, keeping the set of treated places fixed. The placebo coefficients
average zero, which rules out a result produced by the panel's structure but not one
produced by road timing that follows local growth.

A harder case is when *consumers* choose the treatment. @myeong2026bytes estimate what a
food-delivery subscription does to orders, restaurant visits and local spending
(@sec-platform-subscription-spillover). Each user's own sign-up date is the event, so
the identifying variation comes from self-selection plus timing. Their online appendix
contains three checks that carry over to any "adopters versus matched non-adopters"
DiD, and one hazard to look for. (1) *Look-ahead matching.* Compare early adopters with
people who adopt later, using only the window before the later group signs up. Both
groups chose the product, so selection on the decision to subscribe is held fixed and
only its timing differs. Here, the look-ahead comparison (139 users per group) gives
+0.089 focal-platform orders a day, −0.034 rival orders and +0.038 restaurant visits.
All three match the main estimates in sign. The focal and restaurant effects are close
to the main estimates (+0.085 and +0.035), and the rival loss is almost four times
larger (main estimate −0.009), on a far smaller sample. (2)
*A placebo outcome.* Choose an outcome that the treatment should not move but that the
same confounders would move, such as a general spending surge or a change in how the
user uses the app. Non-delivery online spending returns 0.018 (SE 0.013). (3)
*Separate uptake from use.* Dropping subscribers who never ordered, and separately
dropping the heaviest post-subscription users, shows whether the effect is driven by
mechanical usage among the most engaged. Note that the first of these moves the
estimate *toward* treatment-on-the-treated, whatever the table calls it. The hazard is
**bad controls**. The models condition on day-level activity in other spending
categories (beauty, culture, transport, cafés and so on). If those are same-period
spending, as their names suggest (the main text was not available to check), they are
themselves candidate outcomes, and the paper's own thesis is that the subscription
moves non-food local spending. Conditioning on a post-treatment outcome blocks part of
the effect. The no-controls specification is the diagnostic. The platform estimates
barely move (0.704 against 0.706 for log amount), but restaurant visits rise from 0.035
to 0.050, which is the direction that over-control would predict. When the controls
are plausibly affected by treatment, report the specification without them as the
primary estimate, or measure the controls before treatment. A last habit is to check the
stars against the standard errors before quoting an appendix table. Two cells in this
one carry three stars on t-ratios below 1 (−0.012 with SE 0.018 and −0.001 with SE
0.003). These are probably typesetting slips, but a reader cannot know which number is
correct.

In a fifth pattern the event is chosen by a third party. @poelhekke2026acquisitions ask
what a majority acquisition does to the target firm's bank relationships
(@sec-ms-corpdev), where the acquirer picks the target and the target's later bank
choices are the outcome. The design details below come from the main text of the
September 2025 working-paper revision [@poelhekke2025acquisitionswp]; its tables and
online appendix were not read. Four choices are worth copying, and one limit should be
stated plainly. (1) *Difference the outcome when it is a persistent count.* The number
of banks a firm uses barely moves from year to year, so a levels regression with firm
fixed effects has strongly serially correlated errors. The authors regress the change
from the year before the deal to the year after on an acquisition dummy, which removes
the firm effect and also lets the change be split into banks added and banks dropped.
A net change near zero can hide replacement, and the split shows it. (2) *Match by
coarsening, with the lagged outcome matched exactly.* Coarsened exact matching
[@iacus2012cem] puts treated and control firms in the same cell of
year × industry × country and the same bins of employment, revenue, assets, and growth,
and requires the same number of banks before the deal. No propensity model has to be
specified, and balance on the binned variables holds by construction. Three matched
samples of increasing strictness are reported, and the headline estimate (+0.056
relationships in the full sample) is only slightly smaller in each. (3) *Show where
the staggered variation comes from.* A Goodman-Bacon decomposition
[@goodmanbacon2021differencdifferenc] attributes 92% of the identifying variation to
comparisons of treated with never-treated firms, so the forbidden comparisons carry
little weight, and the interaction-weighted estimator [@sun2021eventstudies] and a
same-year-treatment subsample give the same answer. (4) *Report the matched result
when it disagrees.* For acquirers from another region, the full sample shows more banks
added (+0.064) and no change in banks dropped. In the matched sample the addition is no
longer significant and dropped relationships become less likely (−0.029). The authors
print both and change the interpretation from expansion to retention. The limit is
that matching and differencing remove fixed differences and observed pre-deal
characteristics, not selection on what the acquirer expects to happen next. The paper
states its identifying assumption directly, that acquirers do not choose targets on
the trend in the target's bank relationships, and concedes that acquirer motives are
unobserved. The authors also decline to estimate what the new bank ties do to target
performance, because that would require a second source of exogenous variation for
bank choice. Stopping at the estimand the design can support is a choice a reader
should credit.

### From Store Effects to Category Mechanisms: Linking a Survey to a DiD {#sec-causal-did-survey-moderators}

In a sixth pattern the firm chooses where and when to treat, and the question is not
only how large the effect is but why it differs across products. @cetinel2026experience
estimate what opening experience-centric and convenience-centric stores did to an
online-first electronics retailer's revenue (@sec-online-experience-stores). The design
details and numbers here come from the April 2026 working-paper version
[@cetinel2025experiencewp]. Three choices at the store level are worth copying. (1)
*Define exposure the way the decision maker does.* A zipcode is treated if it lies
within a 20-minute travel time of a new store, the retailer's own planning radius. That
gives 192 exposed zipcodes, of which nearest-neighbour propensity-score matching with a
0.1 caliper matches 191, and the results hold under coarsened exact matching
[@iacus2012cem]. (2) *Use the radius as a dose check.* At 25 minutes the two large
stores' short-term revenue uplifts fall from 21.7% and 23.2% to 14.5% and 16.4%. That
is the dilution expected when less-exposed zipcodes join the treated group, and it is
hard to produce with a spurious effect. (3) *Bin event time to match the question.* The
estimator is the interaction-weighted event study of @sun2021eventstudies on log
outcomes with zipcode and month fixed effects and standard errors clustered by zipcode.
Relative time is grouped into three-month bins: the quarter before opening, a
short-term bin covering the opening month and the three months after it, and a
long-term bin for later months. Binning trades resolution for precision on monthly
zipcode data, and the bins name the two horizons the manager asked about.

The category-level model is where the paper is most reusable. A separate coefficient
for each store × category × time bin would use dozens of parameters, each estimated
from one category's noisy sales. The authors instead decompose the effect as
$\gamma_{sck} = \alpha_{sk} + \beta_{ck}$, with $\sum_c \beta_{ck} = 0$, where
$\alpha_{sk}$ is store $s$'s average effect in bin $k$ and $\beta_{ck}$ is category
$c$'s deviation from it, shared across stores. The sum-to-zero constraint does the
identifying work. Without it, any constant could be added to every $\beta_{ck}$ and
subtracted from $\alpha_{sk}$ with no change in fit. It is the same normalization as
effects coding in an analysis of variance, and it makes each $\beta_{ck}$ read as
"how much better than this store's average category." The decomposition then shows that
the store-level average hides a wide spread, from desktops at about 160% to more than
40% of categories with no significant uplift.

The second stage explains that spread with data the sales records cannot provide. In a
preregistered survey (AsPredicted #99412), 450 Prolific respondents from the focal
country rated, for each category, how important each of four benefits was and how much
better a store delivers it than the website. Following the Theory of Reasoned Action,
utility is importance × relative store attractiveness. Sensory experience and product
expertise are averaged into an information-search utility, instant gratification
becomes a fulfilment utility, and return efficiency a returns utility. Categories with
40 or fewer responses are dropped, leaving 22 (16 destination categories and 6
accessories). The authors link the survey to the DiD in two ways. The model-free link
correlates each category's estimated uplift with its utility: $r = .419$ ($p = .052$)
for information search and $r = .504$ ($p = .017$) for total utility, rising to $r =
.575$ ($p = .020$) among destination categories. The integrated link replaces
$\beta_{ck}$ in the short-term bin with $\sum_d \beta_d \, \text{UTILITY}_{cd}$, so that
the utilities enter the DiD itself. A one-standard-deviation increase in
information-search utility multiplies revenue by a factor of 1.085 [1.012, 1.158], and
the same increase in fulfilment utility by 1.090 [1.030, 1.150]. Returns utility does
nothing measurable (1.012). Splitting the categories shows that the effect sits in
destination categories (information search 16.2%, fulfilment 10.1%) and that none of
the accessory coefficients is significant. Accessories still gained from the stores,
which the authors attribute to cross-buying, such as earbuds bought with a phone, and to
use-case displays such as a home-office setup.

A multiplication factor from a log-outcome model is easy to misread. Applied to the
information-search row, where the predicted uplift at mean utility is 54.4%, the factor
multiplies $1 + \text{uplift}$, not the uplift itself.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
# Our toy illustration, not the authors' code: three ways to read a
# "multiplication factor" from a log-outcome DiD. Inputs are the published
# info-search row (working-paper version): predicted short-term uplift of
# 54.4% at mean utility, and a factor of 8.5% per +1 SD of utility.
base   <- 0.544                 # uplift at mean utility: revenue x 1.544
factor <- 0.085                 # +1 SD utility: revenue x 1.085 on top
b_log  <- log(1 + factor)       # the coefficient in log points

readings <- data.frame(
  Reading = c("Correct: multiply (1 + uplift) by the factor",
              "Wrong: scale the uplift itself by the factor",
              "Wrong: add the factor as percentage points"),
  `Uplift at +1 SD (%)` = 100 * c((1 + base) * (1 + factor) - 1,
                                  base * (1 + factor),
                                  base + factor),
  check.names = FALSE
)
readings$`Gain over 54.4% (pp)` <- readings$`Uplift at +1 SD (%)` - 100 * base
knitr::kable(readings, digits = 1)
```

The correct reading reproduces the paper's 67.5%, a gain of 13.1 percentage points.
Scaling the uplift gives 59.0%, and adding the factor gives 62.9%. The underlying
coefficient is 0.082 log points. Because the factor applies to the level of revenue,
the same 8.5% is worth 8.5 points to a category with no baseline uplift and 17.0 points
to one whose revenue has already doubled. A percentage-point gain should therefore always
be reported together with the baseline it was computed from.

The limits of the second stage deserve as much attention as its result. (1) *The sample
is 22 categories.* However many zipcode-months sit behind the first stage, the
explanation rests on 22 points, which is why a correlation of .42 lands at $p = .052$,
and information-search and returns utilities are themselves correlated ($r = .57$), so
separating them leans on a handful of categories. (2) *The link is ecological.* The
utilities are category averages from a general-population panel, not from the
retailer's customers. They show that categories where shoppers value in-store
information gained more, not that the customers who value information are the ones the
store brought in. (3) *Unmeasured supply-side moderators.* Televisions and desktops
beat their predicted uplift, and the retailer's store team explained why: it had
targeted those categories to take share from competitors and staffed them with its
best television salespeople. Store effort varies by category and is invisible to a
consumer survey, so it sits in the residual. The design is still a good template for
"multi-method" work on heterogeneous treatment effects. Estimate the effects with a
structured decomposition, measure the proposed mechanism independently and under
preregistration, report the model-free correlation next to the integrated model, and
use conversations with managers to explain the outliers.

### Two Treated Groups, Two Channels: Platform Sanction or Consumer Boycott? {#sec-causal-did-two-channels}

Some shocks reach an outcome through two parties at once. When an artist is accused
of serious misconduct, listeners may stop listening on purpose, and the streaming
platform may stop promoting the artist. Both happen in the same weeks, both lower
streams, and a difference-in-differences on the artist's streams estimates their sum.
The sum is rarely the quantity anyone needs. A label deciding whether to drop the
artist, a platform defending its content policy, and a regulator weighing
deplatforming rules all need to know which party moved the market.
@winkler2026artist separate the two channels in the case of R. Kelly and the \#MuteRKelly
campaign, and the design is worth learning in detail. They combine
11,501,284 tweets (January 2017 to October 2022), weekly U.S. song-level streams from
Luminate pooled across Spotify, Apple Music and Amazon at the level of the designated
market area (DMA), German streaming data from GfK split into ad-supported and premium
listening, and the 896,749 largest public Spotify playlists, of which 54,498 are
curated by Spotify. The data are not public (the authors gave disguised data to the
editors), so what follows is a reading of the published design rather than a
replication.

*Why the naive comparison misleads.* R. Kelly's streams grew about 2% a year while
the streaming market grew 17%, and the web appendix puts his streams at least 35%
below those of comparable artists. It is tempting to read that gap as a boycott. It
is not evidence of one. The gap combines whatever the platform did, whatever
listeners did, the ordinary aging of a back catalog, and anything else that
separates this artist from the market, and it gives no hint of the shares.

*Two events that move different sides of the market.* On May 10, 2018, Spotify
announced a Hate Content policy and removed R. Kelly from its curated playlists and
its recommendations. The policy was later reversed, but the songs were never put
back on the playlists (they were still absent in 2025). This event changed supply,
meaning what the platform showed listeners, and may also have changed demand. On
January 3, 2019, the documentary *Surviving R. Kelly* aired. Nothing changed on the
platform, while #MuteRKelly tweets rose more than 200-fold. The second event moves
demand-side salience with supply held fixed, which is what makes it useful later.

*Two treated groups with different treatment intensity.* The sanction did not hit
every song equally. Ten songs had been on Spotify-curated playlists and lost that
placement (the delisted songs). Another 349 had never been on a curated playlist,
so they lost only indirect algorithmic exposure (the nondelisted songs). A listener
who boycotts the artist boycotts both kinds of song. Write $\beta$ for the boycott
effect, $\alpha$ for the loss of algorithmic recommendations, and $\nu$ for the loss
of playlist visibility. The two difference-in-differences estimands are then

$$
\tau_{\text{del}} = \beta + \alpha + \nu, \qquad
\tau_{\text{nd}} = \beta + \alpha .
$$ {#eq-47-two-channels}

Two conclusions follow, each with its own assumption. First, because $\alpha$ can
only lower streams, $|\tau_{\text{nd}}|$ is an upper bound on the size of the
boycott effect; the nondelisted estimate may itself be partly algorithmic. Second,
$\tau_{\text{del}} - \tau_{\text{nd}}$ recovers the visibility effect $\nu$ only if
the boycott and algorithmic effects are about the same for both groups. That second
assumption deserves suspicion, because the delisted songs are the hits, and a
boycott could fall harder or more lightly on hits than on deep cuts. The mechanism
tests below are what make it credible.

*Controls, weights, and inference.* Each treated song gets its own matched control
set. The donor pool comes from artists whom Last.fm users listen to alongside
R. Kelly, and controls are matched on pretreatment streams, genre and release
period. There are 320 control songs for the delisted group, 698 for the nondelisted
group and 924 in the pooled sample. Co-listening is a better basis for a donor pool
than a genre label, because control songs then face the same listeners' tastes and
the same seasonal swings. The specification is a two-way fixed-effects regression,

$$
\ln(\text{Streams}_{st}) = \tau\,(\text{Post}_t \times \text{Treat}_s) + \mu_s + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{st},
$$

with song and week fixed effects over seven weeks before and seven weeks after the
event. Two choices matter. Observations are weighted by each treated song's
pretreatment share of the artist's streams, so $\hat\tau$ is an artist-level effect
in which a hit counts for more than a deep cut, rather than an average over songs.
Standard errors are clustered at the matched set, because songs matched to the same
treated song are not independent draws [@abadie2022postmatching]. One risk comes with
a co-listening donor pool. Co-listened artists are substitutes, so streams that leave
R. Kelly may flow to the controls. That violates SUTVA (@sec-causal-week14) and would
make the estimated decline too large. The authors test for this spillover.

Control songs can serve more than one group, which is why the group observation counts sum to more than the pooled count. {#tbl-causal-boycott}

*Reading the estimates.* Across all songs, streams fell about 15% relative to matched
controls (@tbl-causal-boycott). Delisted songs fell about 25%, and nondelisted songs
fell about 4%. On the logic of @eq-47-two-channels, 4.4% is the most that intentional
boycotting could have cost, and the gap between the groups (about 0.24 log points,
our arithmetic) is the visibility effect of losing curated placement. One more
correction matters for interpretation. The outcome pools three services, and Spotify
is about 40% of U.S. streaming, so the authors note that Spotify-specific effects are
roughly 2.5 times larger. Whenever a treatment hits one platform and the outcome is
measured across several, the estimate is diluted by the treated platform's share.

*Dose-response.* If lost visibility drives the decline, songs that lost more curated
reach should lose more streams. The interaction with centered log curated-playlist
followers is −0.1328 (SE 0.0430). "Ignition (Remix)", with more than 5 million curated
followers, fell by about 37%, while "I Believe I Can Fly", with about 250,930, showed
no significant change. The caveat is that curated reach and popularity are highly
correlated (0.781), so on its own the dose test cannot tell visibility apart from a
boycott that hits popular songs harder. That is the job of the next two tests.

*Heterogeneity that points in opposite directions.* Each channel predicts a different
pattern of who leaves. A loss of visibility should mostly affect lean-back listeners
who take what the service plays. In Germany, the decline was concentrated among
ad-supported users. Across U.S. DMAs, proportional declines were larger where
R. Kelly was less popular, that is, among incidental rather than committed listeners.
The documentary shows the reverse gradient. Streams rose more where he was more
popular (by DMA market share and by the share of Black residents), and more for his
less popular songs, while songs featured in the documentary rose less. That is the
signature of existing fans going back to the catalog, not of curious newcomers. One
channel would have to produce both gradients; two channels produce them naturally.

*A second event with no supply change.* The documentary is the demand-side probe. It
is the moment of maximum boycott salience, with no change on the platform, so if
intentional boycotting were a strong channel it should show up here. Streams instead
rose 105% in the week after the broadcast relative to the prior four-week average,
and a difference-in-differences version gives +90%. Negative publicity can raise
sales through awareness [@berger2010negative], and fans can condemn the person while
still consuming the work [@bhattacharjee2013moral]. The authors read this through Hirschman.s distinction
between voice and exit: plenty of voice, little exit. The authors also note that if salience spikes like
this one occurred during the sanction window as well, the supply estimate is, if
anything, understated. Platform-curated visibility, not listener choice, carried
most of the decline.

*Robustness and the descriptive extensions.* The main estimates survive Poisson
models, unweighted OLS, synthetic difference-in-differences [@arkhangelsky2021sdid],
alternative clustering and the bootstrap, a SUTVA-spillover check, and a pretreatment
placebo. The authors then apply SDID to three other cases and are explicit that these
are descriptive. For Morgan Wallen after a racial slur (February 2021; 52 country-artist
donors), the coefficient is 0.814 ($p = 0.081$). For Rammstein in Germany in 2023 (57
donors), it is 0.034 ($p = 0.827$). For Diddy after his arrest (September 2024),
streams peaked about 50% above his own baseline and 60.8% above the synthetic
control. None of these cases has a second treated group, so they show how streams
moved but not which side of the market moved them. A rough calculation for R. Kelly
puts the forgone streams at 900 million to 1.2 billion over 241 weeks, or
\$3.2 million to \$4.2 million in U.S. revenue at \$0.0035 a stream.

*What the design cannot do.* It is one artist, one platform sanction and one
documentary. Without listener-level data, the mechanism evidence comes from aggregate
heterogeneity, and the authors call it suggestive. The documentary estimate combines
media exposure with whatever boycott it prompted, so it bounds the boycott in that
event rather than isolating it. It is also an effect on the audience that remained
after the 2018 sanction, a local effect for that population rather than for everyone
who listened in 2017. The visibility contrast rests on ten delisted songs, which is
few clusters for inference and is why the dose-response and heterogeneity results
carry so much of the argument.

The simulation below sets up the structure of @eq-47-two-channels with known
effects. There are 10 delisted songs with 32 matched controls each, 349 nondelisted
songs with 2 controls each, and 14 weeks, with each matched set sharing its own
trend. The delisted songs differ in how much curated reach they lose.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2018)

# Effects on log weekly streams. Magnitudes are illustrative, not the paper's.
b_boycott <- -0.03   # listeners who choose to stop: every song by the artist
a_algo    <- -0.02   # lost algorithmic recommendations: every song
g_dose    <- -0.06   # lost playlist visibility per unit of curated reach

# One treated group: n_treat songs, each with n_ctrl matched controls that share
# its trend (the reason to match on co-listening). Panel is song x week.
sim_group <- function(n_treat, n_ctrl, dose, weeks = 14, post_from = 8) {
  k     <- 1 + n_ctrl
  set   <- rep(seq_len(n_treat), each = k)
  treat <- rep(c(1, rep(0, n_ctrl)), n_treat)
  dose  <- rep(dose, each = k) * treat
  post  <- matrix(seq_len(weeks) >= post_from, length(set), weeks, byrow = TRUE)
  trend <- outer(rnorm(n_treat, 0, 0.02)[set], seq_len(weeks))
  D     <- treat * post
  Y     <- rnorm(length(set), 8, 1) + trend +
           D * (b_boycott + a_algo + g_dose * dose) +
           matrix(rnorm(length(D), 0, 0.05), nrow(D))
  list(Y = Y, D = D, Dz = D * (dose - mean(dose[treat == 1])), set = set, k = k)
}

# Song effects and set-by-week effects swept out: each treated song is compared
# only with its own matched controls, week by week.
sweep_fe <- function(M, g) {
  setweek <- rowsum(M, g$set) / g$k
  M - rowMeans(M) - setweek[g$set, ] + rowMeans(setweek)[g$set]
}
twfe <- function(g, dose_term = FALSE) {
  X <- cbind(D = c(sweep_fe(g$D, g)))
  if (dose_term) X <- cbind(X, Dz = c(sweep_fe(g$Dz, g)))
  coef(lm.fit(X, c(sweep_fe(g$Y, g))))
}

one_draw <- function() {
  del <- sim_group(10,  32, runif(10, 0.5, 4))  # on curated playlists
  nd  <- sim_group(349,  2, rep(0, 349))        # never on them
  c(nondelisted = twfe(nd)[["D"]], delisted = twfe(del)[["D"]],
    dose_slope = twfe(del, TRUE)[["Dz"]])
}

est <- t(replicate(200, one_draw()))
est <- cbind(est, difference = est[, "delisted"] - est[, "nondelisted"])
truth <- c(b_boycott + a_algo, b_boycott + a_algo + g_dose * 2.25, g_dose,
           g_dose * 2.25)
round(rbind(truth = truth, mean_estimate = colMeans(est),
            sd_across_draws = apply(est, 2, sd)), 3)
#>                 nondelisted delisted dose_slope difference
#> truth                -0.050   -0.185     -0.060     -0.135
#> mean_estimate        -0.050   -0.184     -0.061     -0.134
#> sd_across_draws       0.002    0.021      0.010      0.021
cat("Share of draws in which the nondelisted estimate lies below the true",
    "boycott effect:", mean(est[, "nondelisted"] <= b_boycott), "\n")
#> Share of draws in which the nondelisted estimate lies below the true boycott effect: 1
```
:::


Across 200 simulated datasets, the nondelisted estimate is centered on
$\beta + \alpha = -0.05$, not on the boycott effect of −0.03, and it lies below −0.03
in every draw. That is the upper bound at work: it holds because $\alpha \le 0$, and it
is loose by exactly $|\alpha|$. The delisted-minus-nondelisted difference recovers the
average visibility loss (−0.135), and the dose slope recovers the per-unit effect
(−0.06). The difference is far noisier than the nondelisted estimate, because ten
delisted songs carry it. Two edits break the design in instructive ways. Give the
delisted songs a larger boycott effect than the others and the difference overstates
visibility by that gap. Let control streams rise when treated streams fall (a SUTVA
spillover) and every estimate grows in size.

*A recipe for other settings.* The same structure appears whenever a platform and its
users react to one shock. (1) Name both channels and write each estimand as a sum, as
in @eq-47-two-channels. (2) Find units that share the demand-side exposure (the same
artist, brand or creator) but differ in how much the platform's action touched them,
and estimate each group separately. (3) Build a matched control set for each treated
unit from a behavioral donor pool (co-listening, co-purchase, co-viewing), weight by
pretreatment share if the estimand is at the brand or artist level, and cluster at
the matched set. (4) State the sign assumption behind the bound, and the
equal-boycott assumption behind the difference. (5) Test dose-response in the supply
intensity. (6) Look for heterogeneity that the two channels predict in opposite
directions. (7) Find a second event that moves demand without moving supply. (8) Treat
single-unit synthetic-control or SDID extensions to other cases as description.
@tbl-causal-two-channel-recipe maps the recipe onto settings where it should travel.

| Setting | Supply-side action | High-intensity units | Low-intensity units | Demand-only probe |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Creator deplatforming or demonetization | Platform stops recommending or monetizing a creator | Videos removed from recommendations | Videos reachable only by search or subscription | A news story about the creator with no policy change |
| Marketplace product recall | Marketplace delists or buries recalled items | Recalled SKUs of the brand | The brand's non-recalled SKUs, still listed | Later media coverage of the recall |

The gap between online voice and purchase behavior is not specific to music. After
Goya's CEO praised President Trump in 2020, boycott posts and coverage outweighed
calls to buy in support, yet Goya's sales rose 22% for a short time before fading
within three weeks, with little sign of boycotting among its core customers
(figures from the working-paper abstract of [@liaukonyte2023frontiers]). Together with the case above, it is a reminder that the
volume of a campaign is a poor guide to which side of the market actually moved.


## Instrumental Variables {#sec-causal-iv}

Sometimes treatment is endogenous and no untreated group plausibly satisfies
parallel trends, yet there exists a third variable that shifts the treatment for
reasons unrelated to the outcome. **Instrumental variables** exploit that variable
to isolate the slice of treatment variation that is "as good as randomly assigned."
The motivating problem in marketing is the price endogeneity that defeats naive
demand estimation: observed prices and quantities are jointly determined by demand
and supply, so a regression of quantity on price recovers neither the demand curve
nor a causal price elasticity. An instrument that shifts *supply* (and hence price)
without shifting demand traces out the demand curve.

Let the structural ("second-stage") equation of interest be

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma} + u_i,
$$ {#eq-iv-structural}

where $D_i$ (e.g., price) is correlated with the error $u_i$
($\mathbb{E}[D_i u_i] \neq 0$), so OLS is biased. An instrument $Z_i$ identifies
$\beta_1$ if it satisfies three conditions:

1. **Relevance:** $Z_i$ shifts the treatment, $\operatorname{Cov}(Z_i, D_i) \neq 0$.
   This is testable—it is the first-stage regression.
2. **Exclusion:** $Z_i$ affects $Y_i$ *only* through $D_i$, not directly,
   $\operatorname{Cov}(Z_i, u_i) = 0$. This is untestable and must be argued from
   institutional knowledge.
3. **Exogeneity (independence):** $Z_i$ is as good as randomly assigned with respect
   to the unobservables driving $Y_i$.

The estimator is **two-stage least squares (2SLS)**: regress $D_i$ on $Z_i$ and
covariates to obtain fitted $\hat D_i$ (the exogenous part of treatment variation),
then regress $Y_i$ on $\hat D_i$. With a single instrument and no covariates this
reduces to the Wald ratio,

$$
\hat\beta_1^{\text{IV}}
= \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i, Z_i)}{\operatorname{Cov}(D_i, Z_i)}
= \frac{\widehat{\text{reduced form}}}{\widehat{\text{first stage}}}.
$$ {#eq-wald}

**What IV identifies.** With heterogeneous effects and a binary instrument, 2SLS
does not estimate the ATE but the **local average treatment effect (LATE)**: the
average effect among **compliers**—units whose treatment status responds to the
instrument—under a monotonicity condition (the instrument moves no unit in the
opposite direction). The effect on always-takers and never-takers is not
identified. This is a feature to interpret, not a bug to hide: the LATE answers
"what is the effect for the units a policy operating through this instrument would
actually move?"

**What breaks identification.** Two failures dominate. A **weak instrument** (low
first-stage correlation) inflates variance and, worse, biases 2SLS toward the OLS
estimate it was meant to fix; the conventional diagnostic is a first-stage
$F$-statistic well above the rule-of-thumb of 10, though that threshold is now
known to be optimistic. An **exclusion-restriction violation**—the instrument
affecting the outcome through any channel other than the treatment—biases the
estimate by an amount that *cannot* be detected from the data and must be defended
by argument. In demand estimation the classic instruments are cost shifters and,
following the differentiated-products tradition, functions of rival products'
characteristics that shift a product's markup without entering its demand
directly [@berry1995]. The credibility of any IV study lives or dies on the
narrative for the exclusion restriction.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(47)

# Demand estimation with price endogeneity. A demand shock 'xi' raises BOTH
# quantity and (through the firm's pricing) price -> OLS elasticity is biased
# toward zero. A cost shifter 'Z' instruments for price.
n <- 5000
xi   <- rnorm(n)                              # unobserved demand shock
Z    <- rnorm(n)                              # cost shifter (instrument)
price <- 2.0 - 0.8 * Z + 1.0 * xi + rnorm(n) # price rises with demand shock
true_elasticity <- -1.2
logq <- 5 + true_elasticity * price + 1.5 * xi + rnorm(n)  # xi enters demand

ols <- coef(lm(logq ~ price))["price"]

# 2SLS by hand: first stage, then second stage on fitted price.
first  <- lm(price ~ Z)
phat   <- fitted(first)
iv     <- coef(lm(logq ~ phat))["phat"]
F_stat <- summary(first)$fstatistic["value"]

cat(sprintf("True price elasticity:   %.3f\n", true_elasticity))
#> True price elasticity:   -1.200
cat(sprintf("OLS (biased):            %.3f\n", ols))
#> OLS (biased):            -0.628
cat(sprintf("2SLS (IV):               %.3f\n", iv))
#> 2SLS (IV):               -1.195
cat(sprintf("First-stage F:           %.1f\n", F_stat))
#> First-stage F:           1795.5
```
:::


### Invitations, Not Assignments: Intention-to-Treat Under Two-Sided Non-Compliance {#sec-causal-iv-invitation}

Many good instruments do not assign treatment. They *invite* it. A lottery offers a
voucher that some winners decline. An encouragement design sends an email that some
recipients ignore, while some non-recipients find the feature anyway. Two kinds of
units ignore the instrument. **Never-takers** stay untreated even when invited, and
**always-takers** take treatment even when not invited. The **compliers** are the
units whose treatment the invitation actually moves. With a binary invitation $Z_i$ and
treatment $D_i$, three regressions answer three different questions:

- The reduced form of $Y$ on $Z$ is the **intention-to-treat (ITT)** effect. It is causal
  under nothing more than random assignment of $Z$.
- The first stage of $D$ on $Z$ estimates the share of compliers, $\pi_c$, provided
  there are no defiers.
- Their ratio, @eq-wald, is the LATE on compliers. It additionally needs monotonicity
  and the exclusion restriction.

Because $\text{ITT} = \pi_c \cdot \text{LATE}$ and $0 < \pi_c \le 1$, the ITT has the same
sign as the LATE and is no larger in magnitude. That is what makes it the conservative
headline when the extra assumptions are in doubt.

A study of startups born in the Great Recession [@bias2026recession], covered in
@sec-ent-recession, shows the logic at work. The treatment, being born in the recession, is a founder's
choice. The invitation is receiving one's first patent grant during the recession. Two
independent sources of randomness make it as good as random: examiners who differ in
review speed are assigned quasi-randomly, and nobody filing years earlier could know
when the recession would arrive. That is a *double randomization*, conditioned on
technology-field-by-application-year fixed effects. Two refinements carry over to other
settings. First, the authors found signs that the realized invitation was not quite
random, because weaker applications seemed to get priority during the recession. They
therefore instrumented the realized grant date with a *predicted* grant date, built from
the filing date, the docketing lag, and the examiner's historical speed, and called the
result a bias-corrected ITT. Second, they probed the two assumptions usually waved
through [@bias2023recessionwp]. For exclusion, they ran a "no first stage, no reduced
form" check, due to Angrist, Lavy, and Schlosser. In samples where the invitation does
not move founding dates, such as the untreated firms, it should not move outcomes
either, and it does not. For monotonicity, they used Dobbie, Goldin, and Yang's
implication that with no defiers the first stage must be non-negative in every subsample.
They split startups by inventor-team size, experience, productivity, breakthrough record,
and whether the inventors had an attorney, and the first stage stayed positive throughout.
Their LATEs come out about three times the ITTs, as the complier share implies.

The simulation below builds that population. Always-takers are weaker "forced"
founders and never-takers are stronger ones, so the naive comparison of recession-born
and expansion-born firms mixes types. Here it gets even the *sign* wrong. The ITT is
small but correctly signed, and dividing by the first stage recovers the effect on
compliers.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2007)

# Startups differ in how their founding date responds to a recession-timed
# patent grant Z (the invitation). Type shares loosely follow the working
# paper's compliance decomposition; outcome levels are illustrative only.
n    <- 20000
type <- sample(c("always", "never", "complier"), n, replace = TRUE,
               prob = c(0.20, 0.54, 0.26))
Z    <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3)                           # examiner speed x cycle
D    <- as.integer(type == "always" | (type == "complier" & Z == 1))

# Baseline 7-year survival differs by type (selection), and so does the
# recession effect (heterogeneity). Always-takers are weaker founders.
base   <- c(always = 0.35, never = 0.60, complier = 0.50)[type]
effect <- c(always = 0.05, never = 0.00, complier = 0.30)[type]
Y      <- rbinom(n, 1, pmin(base + effect * D, 1))

ols   <- coef(lm(Y ~ D))["D"]
itt   <- coef(lm(Y ~ Z))["Z"]                       # reduced form
first <- coef(lm(D ~ Z))["Z"]                       # complier share
late  <- itt / first                                # Wald ratio

cat(sprintf("Naive OLS (born in recession vs not): %6.3f\n", ols))
#> Naive OLS (born in recession vs not): -0.068
cat(sprintf("ITT (invited vs not):                 %6.3f\n", itt))
#> ITT (invited vs not):                  0.074
cat(sprintf("First stage (complier share):         %6.3f\n", first))
#> First stage (complier share):          0.257
cat(sprintf("LATE = ITT / first stage:             %6.3f\n", late))
#> LATE = ITT / first stage:              0.287
cat(sprintf("True effect on compliers:             %6.3f\n", 0.30))
#> True effect on compliers:              0.300
```
:::


The LATE describes only the compliers. In the startup study, these are ventures whose
founding date moved with their grant, and the estimate says nothing about the forced
entrepreneurs who would have started in the recession regardless.

The treatment can also be a past *choice*. @gabel2026statedependence use randomly
assigned coupons as the invitation and today's purchase of the couponed brand as the
treatment. The outcome is whether the household buys that brand again on its next
category purchase. The LATE is then the causal effect of one purchase on the next
(structural state dependence) for households that the coupon moved. That is the
parameter that brand-choice models have estimated from observational panels for
decades. The exclusion restriction says the coupon affects next purchase only
through today's purchase. It would fail if the coupon itself made the brand more
memorable. @sec-sm-sd-experiment shows how to compare this LATE with a structural
model's prediction.

An invitation can also expire. In corporate technology pilots the control group is
usually given access once the pilot ends, so the first stage shrinks over calendar time
and eventually vanishes. @cui2026copilot face this in three experiments that randomized
access to an AI coding assistant (@sec-aiml-copilot-rct). In a panel with unit and
period fixed effects, initial assignment $Z_i$ predicts adoption strongly while only the
treated group has access and weakly afterwards. Each additional post-pilot period then
adds noise to a pooled 2SLS estimate without adding identifying variation, and the
analyst is tempted to choose the cutoff date after seeing the results. The authors
instead weight each period by its difference in adoption between treatment and control
[@cui2025copilotwp]. Periods with a large gap count heavily, and periods in which the
control group has caught up count for almost nothing, with no cutoff to choose. The
cost is in the estimand. If the effect of the tool is constant over time, the weights
only improve precision. If it changes, for instance because the tool improves, the
estimate is an average tilted toward the high-gap periods, and that has to be said when
reporting it. The same paper reports the non-experimental difference-in-differences
estimate next to the instrumented one for each firm. The two differ by a factor of about
three, in opposite directions across firms.

When the control group cannot get the treatment at all, there are no always-takers.
The complier share is then simply the take-up rate among the invited, and the effect
on the treated is the ITT divided by that rate. @hicken2026regulatory is a small, clean
example. Working with Thailand's Digital Government Development Agency, they randomized
90 small hotels (100 employees or fewer) that could comment on a draft licensing rule,
blocking on region and the owner's gender. Forty-three were invited to a "RegRoom," an
online session in which a business-law expert explained the draft's public purpose and
reviewed the firms' draft comments. The other 47 received only the standard online
notice-and-comment materials. Seventy-nine percent of invited firms attended. The
paper's 2SLS treatment-on-treated estimates are close to the ITT divided by 0.79. For
perceived regulatory legitimacy on a 0–4 scale, 0.444 / 0.79 = 0.56, against a reported
0.561. For the probability of submitting a comment, 0.323 / 0.79 = 0.41, against a
reported 0.411 and a control rate of 0.191. Doing this division is a quick check on
any reported TOT.

Two other features of the study show up in many field experiments. First, comment
quality exists only for firms that submitted a comment, and the invitation changed which
firms submitted. Of the 90 firms, 31 submitted comments, which three lawyers blind to
treatment status rated. A quality comparison among submitters conditions on a
post-treatment outcome. The authors also report the comparison over all 90 firms, giving
non-submitters the lowest score. That is a well-defined ITT, but on a combined outcome
(submitted, and how well), not an effect on the quality of a given firm's comment.
Second, standard errors are clustered by RegRoom session: the three sessions, plus one
cluster for all control firms and one for invited firms that did not attend. That makes
five clusters, too few for cluster-robust standard errors to be trusted
(@sec-causal-week05). A standard error of 0.0000002 on the period dummy is the visible
symptom. With randomization at the firm level, randomization-inference or wild-cluster-
bootstrap p-values are the check a reader should ask for. One practice is worth
copying. The heterogeneity by baseline views of the state was not in the original
design, and the authors present it as propositions for future tests rather than as
findings.

### Peer Shocks as Instruments: Do Foundations Fill Funding Gaps? {#sec-causal-iv-peer-shock}

Some instruments come from the other agents in a network. A study of large U.S. private
foundations [@lu2026charitable] asks whether a foundation gives a nonprofit more when the
nonprofit needs it more. A development officer asks the same thing when one major funder
pulls back. Need is not observed. The natural proxy is what the recipient's other funders
do: when they cut, the next dollar is worth more to the recipient. But that proxy is
endogenous in the same way price is in demand estimation. A recipient that has a good year,
with a new program or a strong campaign, draws more money from every funder at once. So
foundation $i$'s grant and its peers' grants move together for reasons that have nothing to
do with $i$ responding to need. In the authors' sample, the OLS slope of the change in
$i$'s grant on the change in peer grants is positive.

The instrument is the peers' investment returns. A foundation's giving tracks its
endowment. So when the other foundations funding recipient $j$ earn poor portfolio returns,
they cut their grants to $j$ for reasons unrelated to $j$'s programs. For foundation $i$,
recipient $j$ and year $t$, the outcome is $\Delta\log \text{Grant}_{i,j,t+1}$. The
endogenous regressor is $\Delta\log \text{PeerGrant}_{i,j,t+1}$, the change in what all
other foundations give $j$. The instrument is $\log(1+R_{-i,j,t})$, the return of those
other foundations, weighted by their grants to $j$ over the previous three years. The
regression controls for $i$'s own return, its lagged assets, the current grant and the
current level of peer grants. The own-return control carries the exclusion argument.
Foundations hold similar portfolios, so a bad market year lowers everyone's returns. Without
the control, the instrument would also pick up $i$'s own budget shock.

The responsiveness stops at reallocation. At the foundation level, payout one to three
years ahead does not move with the grant-weighted peer shock across a foundation's
recipients (0.017, SE 0.023, one year ahead). Payout rates also respond about twice as

[@brown2014endowments]. The authors read this as a preference for preserving capital.
Foundations shift a fixed budget toward recipients that need it, but they do not spend
more in total when need rises.

For nonprofit marketing, the result says institutional funders are partial substitutes.
When some cut back, others partly make up the difference, with an elasticity of about
−0.2, and the offset is concentrated in long relationships. That is an empirical case for treating funder retention
as relationship marketing, as @sec-clv does for customers. The replication package ships
the Stata code and de-identified grant extracts, with Candid recipient names replaced by
random identifiers, so the first stage and the splits can be re-estimated.

### The Algorithm's Own Rule as an Instrument: A Recommender's Search Radius {#sec-causal-iv-algorithm-radius}

Platform data invite a particular endogeneity problem. A recommender shows a product
more often *because* the product is appealing, so a regression of clicks on exposure
mixes the effect of being shown with the appeal that got it shown. A study of a mobile
location-based recommender in South Korea [@han2026mlbrs] finds an instrument in the
algorithm's own design. The service, which the authors call SmartAround, ranks nearby
places on proximity, collaborative-filtering popularity and content-based relevance. It
launched officially on April 3, 2019, after a beta for early adopters, and it draws
candidates from a fixed 400-metre radius around the user. When the service switches on,
every restaurant gains exposure, but a restaurant with many rivals inside that radius
splits the gain with them.

The instrument is therefore $\text{Post}_t \times \text{Competitors}_j$, where
$\text{Competitors}_j$ counts other restaurants within 400 m of restaurant $j$ before
the launch. The design resembles a shift-share instrument. The launch is the common
shock, and local density sets each restaurant's share of it. The endogenous regressor
is log exposure, the outcome is log clicks, and every specification carries restaurant
fixed effects, region-by-time and category-by-time fixed effects, district daily active
users and weather. The first stage is negative, as dilution predicts (−0.000394 per
rival in log exposure), and strong (Kleibergen–Paap $F = 316$ on 3.7 million
restaurant-days from 16,720 restaurants in ten districts). The 2SLS elasticity of
clicks with respect to exposure is 0.078 (SE 0.009).

The outer rings carry the exclusion argument, and they work because the cutoff is known.
The radius is centred on the user, not the restaurant. A rival 400–800 m away can
therefore still enter the candidate set of a user standing between the two, so the
inner rings absorb some of the mechanism along with neighbourhood confounding. The
authors treat the resulting 0.062 as a conservative bound. A rival 800 m or more away
can never share a candidate set with the focal restaurant, so the 800–1,000 m and
800–1,200 m rings are clean negative controls, and with them the estimate stays at
0.077 to 0.078. Two limits are stated openly. The first stage collapses under
district-by-time fixed effects ($F = 15.5$, estimate insignificant), because those
absorb most of the cross-district variation the instrument relies on. The maintained
assumption is that no unobserved confounder operates only inside the 400 m radius.

The funnel continues to visit intentions (calls, saves, navigation requests), and here
the design asks more of the reader. The visit equation uses the *fitted* log clicks
from the click stage as its regressor, which gives 0.053 (SE 0.002) with $F = 6{,}587$.
The appendix also reports that the instrument does not predict visits in reduced form
(3.05e−7, $p = 0.548$) and offers this as support for the exclusion restriction. A
referee should read it the other way. If the instrument moves exposure, exposure moves
clicks and clicks move visits, the reduced form of the instrument on visits must be the
product of the three stages. @eq-wald says a just-identified IV estimate is the reduced
form divided by the first stage, so with this instrument alone a null reduced form
implies a null visit effect. A visit-stage $F$ in the thousands, beside a click-stage
$F$ of 316, suggests the fitted clicks carry variation beyond the instrument. One
possibility is that they come from observed rather than instrumented exposure, which
would let restaurant appeal back in. The appendix wording leaves this open, and the main
text may settle it. Until it does, treat 0.078 as the identified result and 0.053 as
less secure.

The simulation below builds the design. Restaurants sit in neighbourhoods of varying
density, appeal raises exposure and clicks together, and busier neighbourhoods gain
more app users after launch. The instrument alone is biased by that neighbourhood
shock. An outer-ring control or neighbourhood fixed effects remove most of the bias.
The last lines contrast two ways to estimate the visit stage, and compare the reduced
form with what the chain of effects predicts.

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(400)

# Pre-to-post changes for restaurants in 60 neighbourhoods (restaurant fixed
# effects differenced out). Effect sizes are illustrative, not the paper's.
n_hood <- 60
n      <- 20000
hood   <- sample(n_hood, n, replace = TRUE)
dens   <- rgamma(n_hood, shape = 4, rate = 0.4)[hood]     # neighbourhood density
comp   <- rpois(n, dens)                                   # rivals within 400 m
ring   <- rpois(n, 5 * dens)                               # rivals 800-1,200 m
eta    <- 0.03 * (dens - 10) + rnorm(n_hood, 0, 0.1)[hood] # post-launch demand
appeal <- rnorm(n)                                         # unobserved appeal

d_exp   <- 1.5 - 0.10 * comp + 0.5 * appeal + 0.3 * eta + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
d_click <- b_click * d_exp + 0.6 * appeal + 0.5 * eta + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
d_visit <- b_visit * d_click + 0.4 * appeal + 0.2 * eta + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)

# Just-identified 2SLS as the Wald ratio of reduced form to first stage.
wald <- function(y, d, z, w = rep(0, length(z))) {
  fs <- lm(d ~ z + w); rf <- lm(y ~ z + w)
  c(est = unname(coef(rf)["z"] / coef(fs)["z"]),
    F   = unname(summary(fs)$coefficients["z", "t value"]^2),
    rf  = unname(coef(rf)["z"]), fs = unname(coef(fs)["z"]))
}
demean <- function(v) v - ave(v, hood)

ols      <- coef(lm(d_click ~ d_exp))["d_exp"]
iv_raw   <- wald(d_click, d_exp, comp)
iv_ring  <- wald(d_click, d_exp, comp, ring)
iv_fe    <- wald(demean(d_click), demean(d_exp), demean(comp))
vis_iv   <- wald(d_visit, d_click, comp, ring)
plug     <- fitted(lm(d_click ~ d_exp + ring))   # fitted from OBSERVED exposure
vis_plug <- coef(lm(d_visit ~ plug + ring))["plug"]
chain    <- iv_ring["fs"] * b_click * b_visit

cat(sprintf("Exposure -> clicks, true:             %7.3f\n", b_click))
#> Exposure -> clicks, true:               0.300
cat(sprintf("  OLS:                                %7.3f\n", ols))
#>   OLS:                                  0.605
cat(sprintf("  2SLS, instrument alone:             %7.3f  (F = %.0f)\n", iv_raw["est"], iv_raw["F"]))
```
