The plug-in visit estimate inherits the appeal bias of OLS, however large its $F$. The
reduced form on visits is small but not zero, and close to the product of the stages. Neighbourhood fixed effects work here because rival counts vary a good deal
within a neighbourhood. In the paper they vary too little within a district, which is
why district-by-time fixed effects drained the first stage.

The template carries over to other platform settings. Find a rule the algorithm
follows, such as a radius, a ranking cutoff, a rotation or a capacity, and combine it
with the moment the rule took effect. Then use the rule's known limits to build negative
controls, units the algorithm can never reach. For the substantive findings on
geographically disadvantaged restaurants, see @sec-online-mobile-recs.

### Two Instruments, Two Complier Groups: A Prompt and a Stock-Out {#sec-causal-iv-two-instruments}

Most IV papers defend one instrument. A study of "swap and save" prompts in online
grocery shopping [@gonzalvez2026swapsave] uses two for the same treatment, and the
pair shows what a second instrument can and cannot add. The substantive question
(@sec-nudge-identification) is whether a shopper who accepts a prompted swap to a
cheaper product keeps buying it. The treatment is the swap, the outcome is buying the
alternative on later trips, and the endogeneity is self-selection: shoppers who accept
a swap may be the ones who would have drifted to that product anyway. The setting is
an Israeli price-comparison platform covering five online supermarkets in 2015, and
the category is mineral water.

The first instrument is exposure to the button. The authors compare shoppers who were
shown it (4,079, including those who clicked and declined and those who never
clicked) with matched shoppers who bought the same product at the same store within
30 days and were not shown it (1,905), in an event-study panel with shopper, retailer,
day-of-week and trip fixed effects. The second instrument is a stock-out of the
shopper's regular water, when the same button offers in-stock substitutes regardless
of price. @tbl-ci-swap-iv sets the two side by side.

| | Prompt exposure | Stock-out |
|:---|:---|:---|
| What moves the shopper | A cheaper alternative is flagged | The regular product is unavailable |
| First stage | 0.369 (SE 0.012), $F = 890$ | 0.535 (SE 0.046), $F = 136$ |
| Effect of a swap on later purchase | 0.214 (SE 0.027) | 0.318 (SE 0.070) |
| Observations | 27,682 | 9,745 |
| Independence argument | Day-to-day price movements decide who sees a prompt; pre-trends flat | Supply disruptions decide who meets a stock-out; pre-trends flat |
| Main exclusion threat | The prompt advertises the alternative even to shoppers who decline | The stock-out recurs, or changes how the shopper views the regular product |

: Two instruments for the same treatment, from the online appendix of @gonzalvez2026swapsave. Standard errors are clustered by shopper, and both first stages report the Kleibergen–Paap $F$. The main text has not been read for this summary. {#tbl-ci-swap-iv}

Three features of the design are worth carrying to other settings.

*One-sided non-compliance changes the estimand.* A shopper cannot swap without the
button, so the prompt design has no always-takers. In that case the LATE of
@sec-causal-iv is the effect of treatment on the treated: the compliers are exactly
the shoppers who swapped. The IV estimate (21.4 points) and the authors' matched
difference-in-differences on swappers (23.7 points in the abstract) therefore target
the same group, and their agreement is a real cross-check on the selection story, not
two unrelated numbers that happen to be close. The implied intention-to-treat effect
of showing the button, first stage times second stage, is about 8 points. A platform
deciding whether to deploy the button to everyone needs that figure, while a brand
asking what one trial is worth needs the 21.

*An exclusion threat that can be partly tested.* A prompt could raise later purchases
without a swap, simply by putting the alternative in front of the shopper. The
appendix checks this in two ways. Exposed shoppers who did not swap are no more
likely than unexposed controls to buy the alternative afterwards ($-0.010$, not
significant). And a heteroskedasticity-based instrument in the style of Lewbel (2012)
frees the prompt to enter the outcome equation directly, where its coefficient is
$-0.036$ (SE 0.013). Both point away from an advertising effect. If anything the
second suggests that seeing and declining an offer makes a later purchase slightly
less likely, which would bias the main estimate down. Neither check covers everything.
The first speaks only for never-takers, since a direct effect among the shoppers who
did swap cannot be separated from the swap itself, and the second leans on the
Lewbel estimator's own assumptions about the error structure.

*Different instruments answer for different shoppers.* The stock-out estimate (31.8
points) is half again as large as the prompt estimate. The two confidence intervals
overlap, so the gap may be noise. If it is real, it has an interpretation: shoppers
who accept a price-motivated swap are selected on price sensitivity, while a
stock-out pushes a broader set of shoppers into a trial. Agreement between two
instruments is evidence for both, but disagreement is not evidence against either,
because each recovers the effect for its own compliers. The stock-out result carries
the paper's mechanism claim for a different reason. It involves no price advantage,
so persistence after it cannot be a response to savings. Its exclusion restriction
needs its own scrutiny. A stock-out that recurs on later trips would raise purchases
of the substitute mechanically, and the appendix asserts that stock-outs are
temporary without reporting how often they repeat.

Two measurement choices sit under both designs. Exposure is inferred for shoppers who
never clicked: the button is taken as shown if another shopper triggered a swap for
that product at that store on that day. The alternative product for anyone who did
not swap is imputed as the most common swap target. Misclassified exposure weakens a
first stage, and these first stages are strong, but a reader should still ask whether
the unexposed controls were unexposed.

The simulation shows the first and third points. Price-sensitive shoppers accept
prompted swaps, drift toward cheap products anyway, and are less likely to stay once
the price edge is gone. Stock-out swaps are unrelated to price sensitivity.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2015)

# Shoppers differ in price sensitivity s. Price-sensitive shoppers are the ones
# who accept a cheaper swap, they drift toward cheap products anyway (baseline),
# and they are less likely to stay with a product once its price edge is gone.
# All magnitudes are illustrative, not the paper's.
n    <- 200000
s    <- runif(n)
base <- 0.05 + 0.10 * s            # later purchase of the alternative, no trial
tau  <- 0.35 - 0.25 * s            # effect of one trial on later purchase

wald <- function(y, d, z) (mean(y[z == 1]) - mean(y[z == 0])) /
                          (mean(d[z == 1]) - mean(d[z == 0]))

# Instrument 1: the prompt. No button, no swap (one-sided non-compliance),
# and only the price-sensitive accept.
z1 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
d1 <- z1 * (s > 0.63)
y1 <- rbinom(n, 1, base + tau * d1)

# Instrument 2: a stock-out. Whether a shopper takes the suggested substitute
# depends on things unrelated to price sensitivity.
z2 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.1)
d2 <- z2 * rbinom(n, 1, 0.535)
y2 <- rbinom(n, 1, base + tau * d2)

naive <- mean(y1[z1 == 1 & d1 == 1]) - mean(y1[z1 == 1 & d1 == 0])

cat(sprintf("Prompt: share of exposed who swap        %6.3f\n", mean(d1[z1 == 1])))
#> Prompt: share of exposed who swap         0.371
cat(sprintf("  Swappers vs. exposed non-swappers      %6.3f\n", naive))
#>   Swappers vs. exposed non-swappers       0.196
cat(sprintf("  Wald estimate, prompt as instrument    %6.3f\n", wald(y1, d1, z1)))
#>   Wald estimate, prompt as instrument     0.151
cat(sprintf("  True effect on those who swapped       %6.3f\n", mean(tau[d1 == 1])))
#>   True effect on those who swapped        0.146
cat(sprintf("Stock-out: share of exposed who swap     %6.3f\n", mean(d2[z2 == 1])))
#> Stock-out: share of exposed who swap      0.534
cat(sprintf("  Wald estimate, stock-out as instrument %6.3f\n", wald(y2, d2, z2)))
#>   Wald estimate, stock-out as instrument  0.223
cat(sprintf("  True effect on those who swapped       %6.3f\n", mean(tau[d2 == 1])))
#>   True effect on those who swapped        0.225
cat(sprintf("Average effect in the population         %6.3f\n", mean(tau)))
#> Average effect in the population          0.225
```
:::


Comparing swappers with exposed non-swappers overstates the effect, because swappers
would have bought the alternative more often in any case. The prompt instrument
recovers the effect on the shoppers who swapped, which here is below the population
average. The stock-out instrument recovers the population average because its
compliers are a random draw. Both are correct, and they differ. The ordering in the
simulation matches the paper's two estimates, but that is one story that fits them,
not something the appendix establishes.

### A Policy List as an Instrument: Offshoring and Innovation {#sec-causal-iv-policy-list}

Governments often liberalize by list: these products may now be imported, these
sectors may now take foreign investment. Membership on the list is a tempting
instrument, because it shifts what firms do in some categories and not in others.
@branstetter2026offshoring use one to ask whether offshoring production reduces
innovation. In November 2001 Taiwan removed 122 electronics products from the list of
goods whose production could not be moved to mainland China. The data cover 483 listed
Taiwanese electronics firms in 16 product clusters, and @sec-innovation-offshoring
describes the measures and the findings. This section looks at the design, using the
working-paper version [@branstetter2021offshoringwp], the only one whose tables were
available here.

For firm $i$, product cluster $j$ and horizon $t$ from 2003 to 2011, the two stages
are

$$
\Delta \ln \text{Off}_{ijt} = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1\,\text{Affected}_j + \varepsilon_{ijt},
\qquad
\Delta \ln \text{Pat}_{ijt} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\widehat{\Delta \ln \text{Off}}_{ijt} + u_{ijt},
$$ {#eq-iv-policy-list}

where $\Delta$ is the change from 2000 to year $t$, $\text{Off}$ is the cumulated
export value of the firm's mainland subsidiaries in the cluster, $\text{Pat}$ is the
firm's weighted patent count in the cluster, and one is added before taking logs.
$\text{Affected}_j$ equals one if the cluster was liberalized. Each horizon is a
separate regression on 3,665 firm-cluster pairs, with standard errors clustered by
firm. Long differences are used because the customs data begin in 2000, which leaves
one year before the reform.

Ordinary least squares gives a coefficient between +0.005 and +0.008 at the horizons
through 2008. Two-stage least squares gives −0.023 to −0.032 at the five horizons
where it is significant. The authors' explanation is a demand shock: a firm whose
product is selling well expands production in China and also invests in the
technology behind it, which pushes the OLS coefficient up.

With one binary instrument and no covariates, @eq-iv-policy-list is a Wald ratio:

$$
\hat\beta_1 = \frac{\overline{\Delta \ln \text{Pat}}_{\text{affected}} - \overline{\Delta \ln \text{Pat}}_{\text{unaffected}}}
                   {\overline{\Delta \ln \text{Off}}_{\text{affected}} - \overline{\Delta \ln \text{Off}}_{\text{unaffected}}}.
$$ {#eq-iv-policy-wald}

The design is therefore a comparison of patent growth in liberalized and
non-liberalized clusters, scaled by the difference in offshoring growth. Anything else
that made patenting grow at different rates in the two groups of clusters is in the
numerator. @tbl-iv-policy-list goes through the checks this implies.

| Question | What the working paper reports | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Is the first stage strong? | $F$ between 22.8 and 45.9 in the full sample (Table 4) | Strong in the full sample |
| Does it stay strong in subsamples? | In clusters that were product-oriented before the reform, $F$ is 1.9 to 4.2 for 2003–2006 and 12.6 to 15.1 for 2007–2011 (Table 10) | The claim that the decline is driven by product-oriented clusters rests on a weak first stage at the early horizons |
| Do pre-trend controls change the estimate? | Controlling for 1995–1999 global patenting trends, $F$ is 5.1 to 7.7 through 2006 and the significant coefficients are −0.087 to −0.137 (Table A3.1) | Sign survives; the magnitude is about four times the baseline and the early horizons are weakly identified |
| At what level does the instrument vary? | 16 product clusters; errors clustered on 483 firms. An instrumental-variable Poisson model with product-clustered errors is negative at every horizon (Table 7) | Firm clustering treats cluster-level assignment as if it varied across thousands of pairs; with 16 clusters, cluster-robust errors are themselves unreliable |
| How were the units defined? | 669 HS codes grouped by K-means on 2000–2011 patents, 2000–2011 exports, and the policy indicator. Results are also shown for two other distance measures and for 18 clusters (Tables A3.3–A3.5) | Units are built from the instrument and post-reform outcomes; with Euclidean distance the estimate is significant at three horizons only |
| Is there a pre-period for the treatment? | Customs data start in 2000 | No pre-trend test for offshoring is possible, which the authors acknowledge |
| Is the exclusion restriction plausible? | China joined the WTO in late 2001; the liberalized list leans toward high-technology products | Authors argue the WTO shock was common to one sector and that technological opportunity would bias toward a positive effect; U.S. patenting in the affected classes was catching up over the period (Appendix A2) |

: Design checks for the policy-list instrument in the Taiwan offshoring study, from the working paper [@branstetter2021offshoringwp]. {#tbl-iv-policy-list}

Three lessons apply to any list-based instrument.

First, count the units at which the instrument varies. A list assigns treatment to
categories, and there are rarely many of them. Thousands of firm-category observations
do not add independent variation in the instrument. With few assigned units, report
inference that respects the assignment level, such as a wild cluster bootstrap or a
permutation of which categories are treated, next to the conventional errors.

Second, a strong first stage in the full sample says nothing about a subsample.
Heterogeneity analysis in IV re-estimates the first stage on each split, and one split
can be weak when the pooled sample is not. Report the first-stage $F$ for every split
and treat a weak one as uninformative, whatever its coefficient.

Third, fix the units before looking at outcomes. When categories must be aggregated,
aggregate them on pre-period information only. Grouping on post-period outcomes and
on the instrument makes the comparison groups a function of the result.

The estimate is a local average effect for firm-cluster pairs whose mainland exports
rose because the product was liberalized. The sample keeps 483 of 792 listed
electronics firms, those with at least some patenting or mainland exporting, so it
describes the larger multinational firms and not the sector as a whole.

### Infrastructure Rollout as a Source of Variation: The Broadband Literature {#sec-causal-iv-broadband}

Few treatments have been used as often as the arrival of broadband. The outcomes
differ from paper to paper (shopping trips, retailer exit, music piracy, voter
turnout, wages, hate crime, body weight, test scores), but the identification problem
is always the same. Providers and regulators decide where and when the network is
built, and they build first where they expect subscribers. A regression of an outcome
on local broadband therefore compares places that differ in income, density,
education and demand for the very things the outcome measures. Each paper has to find
some part of the variation in broadband that is not a response to local demand.
@tbl-causal-broadband-lit lists a set of published studies, with the source of
variation and the design given only as far as each paper's abstract states them.

Read by its third column, the table sorts into five sources of variation. The first
is the topology of the network that was there before broadband: digital subscriber
lines ran over telephone wire, so the layout of the old telephone and cable networks
shaped where fast service could be offered [@falck2014elections; @czernich2011broadband].
The second is the cost of building, which depends on terrain and distance: slope
[@raj2026broadband] and, in the worked example below, district land area. The third is
rationing, where a public program or subsidy auction decides who is served first
[@akerman2015skill]. The fourth is the arrival of backbone capacity, such as a
submarine cable landing on a coast, whose timing is set far from the places studied
[@hjort2019fast; @dandrea2024highspeed]. The fifth is the timing of diffusion itself,
with fixed effects absorbing level differences between places
[@tran2026broadband; @vigdor2014scaling]. Each source needs its own exclusion
argument. Telephone topology must affect turnout only through the Internet; slope must
affect retailer survival only through broadband, and not through the transport costs
and population density that also follow terrain.

For marketing, the outcomes are as instructive as the designs. @tran2026broadband
finds modest average effects of broadband on consumer packaged goods shopping, with
sharp declines in brick-and-mortar shopping among younger consumers and stability in
the larger older cohorts. @raj2026broadband finds that broadband lowered the
probability that a physical retailer exited, in a period before e-commerce was a
serious competitor, and attributes the effect to lower consumer search costs.
@falck2014elections and @gavazza2019internet both report that broadband displaced
other media (television in Germany, radio and newspapers in the U.K.) and lowered
turnout. These are channel-substitution and media-substitution results of the kind
marketing studies directly.

Education is where the literature disagrees most. @belo2014broadband find that heavy
broadband use in Portuguese schools lowered exam grades, and that students did
relatively better in schools that blocked sites such as YouTube. @vigdor2014scaling
find modest negative effects of home computer technology on math and reading scores.
@dettling2018every find that residential broadband raised SAT performance and college
applications, mainly among high-SES students. @chen2021internet find that district
internet spending is associated with better academic indicators and also with a 5%
rise in one class of disciplinary problems. These studies do not estimate the same
treatment. Classroom use intensity, a home computer, broadband available in a postal
code and district spending are four different interventions, and the signs need not
agree. A paper entering this literature adds most when it says precisely which
treatment it is estimating.

#### A worked example: access and speed in U.S. school districts

@niewoehner2026broadband separate two treatments that earlier work had combined:
whether households have broadband (access) and how fast the available connection is
(speed). The outcome, the share of students in grades 3–8 scoring proficient or above
on state math assessments, is one that marketing and operations papers on broadband had
not studied. The figures below come from the working-paper version
[@niewoehner2025broadbandwp]; its main estimates match the published abstract.

The panel covers more than 6,800 school districts in 33 states from 2017 to 2022, with
no tests in 2019–20. Each district follows the cohort that was in third grade in 2017.
Access is the share of households subscribing to broadband in the American Community
Survey, and the paper also uses the range of that share across Census tracts within a
district as a measure of the district's internal digital divide. Speed is the maximum
advertised download speed in FCC Form 477 filings at the Census-block level,
winsorized and logged. The model is a value-added specification,

$$
Y_{it} = \phi_1 Y_{i,t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{i,t-2} + \beta D_{it}
       + \mathbf{x}_{it}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma} + \eta_i + \delta_t + \varepsilon_{it},
$$ {#eq-broadband-va}

where $Y_{it}$ is proficiency in district $i$ and year $t$, $D_{it}$ is the broadband
measure, $\mathbf{x}_{it}$ holds controls for population density, enrollment, adult
education and unemployment, within-state income quartile and local school revenue,
$\eta_i$ is a district effect and $\delta_t$ a year effect.

A lagged outcome and a district effect cannot both be handled by the within
estimator, because demeaning makes the lag correlated with the error. The authors use
one-step System GMM [@blundell1998]. It stacks two sets of equations: first
differences, which remove $\eta_i$ and use lagged levels as instruments, and levels,
which keep $\eta_i$ and use lagged differences as instruments. Lagged proficiency is
treated as endogenous and broadband as predetermined, and the instrument matrix is
collapsed to 31 instruments to limit instrument proliferation. Two excluded
instruments are added: the log of the district's land area, a proxy for the cost of
deployment, and the share of district area covered by broadband.

Land area enters only the level equation, and the reason is the most reusable point
in the paper. A variable that never changes over time is zero after first
differencing, so it cannot instrument anything in the differenced equation. In the
level equation the error contains $\eta_i$, so the instrument must be uncorrelated
with the district's persistent level of proficiency, given the controls. That is a
strong requirement. Large districts are rural, and rurality affects school finance,
transport and teacher labor markets as well as the cost of laying fiber. The
argument therefore rests on the density, income and revenue controls. The
Difference-in-Hansen tests for the land-area and coverage instruments ($p > 0.23$ and
$p > 0.24$) check these moments only on the assumption that the remaining ones are
valid, and Hansen tests lose power as instruments multiply. The paper also reports
Kleibergen–Paap and Anderson–Rubin statistics for instrument strength in its appendix,
which is good practice when the weak-instrument problem of @staiger1997instrumenvariables
is in play.

For all students, the access coefficient is 0.545 (s.e. 0.145): a one-point increase
in the share of households with broadband goes with a 0.545-point increase in the
share proficient, 1.22% of the 44.7% baseline. The working paper's abstract and
introduction describe this as more than a one-point (1.22 percentage-point) gain; the
published abstract has it right. Keep
percentage points and percent apart in your own abstracts. The lag coefficients are
0.515 and 0.295, AR(2) has $p = 0.176$ and the Hansen test $p = 0.161$, on 27,428
observations from 6,832 districts with standard errors clustered by state. The
within-district range has a negative coefficient ($-0.0644$), so the internal digital
divide matters as well as the average. Speed enters as a quadratic in log speed with
coefficients 0.0591 and $-0.00432$, an inverted U.

b2 <- -0.00432

#> Slope at 25 Mbps relative to slope at 100 Mbps: 1.62

#> Long-run multiplier 1/(1 - phi1 - phi2): 5.26

            0.545 / (1 - sum(phi))))

The chunk is our own arithmetic on the reported coefficients. The turning point is
$-0.0591 / (2 \times -0.00432) = 6.84$ in log Mbps, about 935 Mbps, just below a
gigabit. The paper places it at the 16th percentile of the speed distribution, so most
districts lie on the declining side. The table reports effects in the units of the
outcome as the paper scales it. The slope at 25 Mbps is 1.62 times the slope at 100
Mbps, and moving from the peak to 2,000 Mbps lowers the predicted outcome by only
0.0025 in those units in a single period. A quadratic fitted where 84% of the data
lie past the peak gets most of its curvature from the declining side and imposes
symmetry on the rising side. The authors' spline check (knots at the 15th and 75th
percentiles) is the right complement: it finds a positive slope at low speeds and
negative slopes in the middle and upper ranges. One caution in that table is that the
spline model for disadvantaged students fails the AR(2) test ($p = 0.025$).

Two more pieces of arithmetic are worth doing on any value-added model. The
coefficient $\beta$ is the effect in one period with last period's proficiency held
fixed. If the effect persisted, the lag polynomial implies a long-run multiplier of
$1/(1 - 0.515 - 0.295) = 5.26$, so 0.545 would cumulate to 2.87. A cohort observed
from third to eighth grade never reaches that steady state, so 2.87 is an upper bound
from the arithmetic, not an estimate.

The paper's second design is closer to an experiment. In the 2018 Connect America Fund
Phase II reverse auction, the FCC subsidized deployment in eligible areas. Among
eligible areas with a winning bid, some schools received service in 2018–19 and others
later, with timing driven by the provider's engineering lead times, capacity and local
frictions. Comparing early with later deployment in a matched difference-in-differences
across 24 states, the authors find that deployment above the baseline standard,
including gigabit service, lowered math proficiency by about 4 percentage points,
while deployment at the baseline standard (at least 25/3 Mbps) produced modest gains,
significant in one sample. Conditioning on having won a bid removes the question of
who gets subsidized; what remains is the claim that, among winners, the timing of
construction is unrelated to trends in proficiency. That is the not-yet-treated logic
of staggered designs (@sec-causal-week06), with later-served schools as controls
[@callaway2021did].

The two designs differ in size as well as method. The quadratic implies that going
from the peak to 2,000 Mbps changes the outcome by $-0.0025$ per period in its own
units, which is considerably smaller than four percentage points under either reading
of the scale, even after the long-run multiplier. The two estimates answer different
questions. One is the effect of a marginal change in the fastest speed advertised
somewhere in a district; the other is the effect of a discrete gigabit build reaching
a school. A reader should not use one to validate the magnitude of the other.

The paper adds several checks. A state-by-state jackknife leaves the access estimate
stable; dropping Massachusetts raises it by about 11%. In Minnesota, the only state
with historical school attendance zones, a school-level version gives an access
coefficient of 0.307 ($p < 0.01$) and no clear inverted U, because most blocks there
already have gigabit service. For reading (ELA) there is no consistent overall
effect, though English learners show an inverted U with a turning point near 2 Gbps.
The access effect is largest in the early grades and declines through middle school.

Three threats are common to the whole genre, and this paper illustrates each of them.

First, rollout follows demand. Any variation left after controls reflects where
providers expected subscribers. Topology, terrain, rationing and backbone timing are
attempts to find variation that providers did not choose, and the CAF II comparison
is an attempt to compare places all of which were selected.

Second, adoption is not availability. The ACS subscription share is a demand
measure: households subscribe because of income, education, children's needs and
taste, all of which predict test scores. With an availability-based instrument the
estimate is a local effect for households whose subscription responds to supply, in
the sense of @sec-causal-iv. A regression of the outcome on availability alone would
be an intention-to-treat estimate, and the two should not be confused.

Third, advertised speed is not delivered speed. Form 477 records the fastest tier a
provider says it could offer in a block, and a block counts as served if one location
in it can be. Students experience delivered throughput, shared among siblings and
devices. Measurement error in a variable that also enters squared does not simply
attenuate, so the location of the turning point carries this error as well as
sampling error. A turning point should be reported with a confidence interval
(delta method or Fieller), not only as a number.

A smaller point is inference. With 33 states, state-clustered standard errors are
near the range where cluster-robust inference becomes unreliable, and the jackknife by
state is a useful addition for that reason.

The general lesson for a marketing paper that uses broadband, or any other
infrastructure, as a source of variation: name the treatment (availability, adoption,
use or speed), name where its variation comes from and why that source is unrelated
to local demand, and check whether the outcome you study could also be moved by the
same source through another channel.

### Exposure to a Talent Supply: University Hiring Networks as an Instrument {#sec-causal-iv-talent-network}

@babina2024ai want the effect of a firm's AI investment, measured as the change in
its share of AI-skilled workers from 2010 to 2018, on its growth
(@sec-aiml-ai-firm-growth). OLS is suspect for two reasons. Firms that expect growth
may hire AI workers in anticipation, and an unobserved demand shock may raise both AI
hiring and sales. The instrument uses a supply constraint. AI talent was scarce in the
2010s, and the universities that were already strong in AI research turned out more
AI-trained graduates once commercial interest arrived around 2012. A firm that
habitually hired from those universities could recruit AI workers more easily.

The instrument has the exposure form familiar from shift-share designs:

$$
IV_i = \sum_u s^{2010}_{iu}\, AIstrong_u,
$$ {#eq-causal-iv-talent}

where $s^{2010}_{iu}$ is the share of firm $i$'s 2010 STEM workers who graduated from
university $u$ (over the firm's 50 largest source universities) and $AIstrong_u$ marks
universities that, in some year from 2005 to 2009, were in the top 5% by count of AI
researchers in the Open Academic Graph, or in the top 10% by count and top 5% by AI
share of researchers. The shares come from resumes; the shock comes from publication
records that predate the commercial boom.

The general theory of these instruments says identification can come from the shares
or from the shocks [@goldsmithpinkham2020bartik; @borusyak2022shiftshare]. Here the
shock is a fixed university attribute, so it does not vary over time, and the argument
rests on the shares: conditional on controls, firms whose hiring networks ran through
AI-strong universities must not have been on different growth paths for other reasons.
The obvious threat is that AI-strong universities are also strong at everything else,
so exposure to them proxies for hiring from elite or technical schools. The authors
build two parallel exposures with the same 2010 shares, one to universities strong in
non-AI computer science and one to the U.S. News top 10, and control for both in every
specification. The design then compares firms with the same exposure to computer
science and to prestige but different exposure to AI research specifically.

The rule recovers all 44 AI-strong universities in the kit's flag, led by Carnegie

flags four more: Drexel, UC Riverside, Central Florida, and Wisconsin–Madison. Each

it assigns researchers to their institution in years when they did not publish, and
the posted panel may not include that adjustment. The paper's statements about overlap
with rankings reproduce exactly: half of the U.S. News top 20 and 39% of the top 50
are AI-strong, and a quarter of the AI-strong universities are in the top 20. The
validation that OAG researcher counts track university R&D spending also reproduces
(correlation 0.83).

The kit's firm-level regression file is a different matter. Compustat is replaced by
pseudo data. Running the published Table 3 specification on it gives −0.03 for sales
and −0.17 for employment, against the published 0.202 and 0.239, on 995 rather than
1,052 firms. The code runs, but the coefficients have nothing to do with the paper's.
This is common in finance replication kits, and a reader who reruns one should check
which inputs were replaced before calling the result a replication.

Three lessons carry over to exposure instruments in marketing, where similar
designs measure exposure to a media market, a supplier, or a platform's rollout.

First, an exposure instrument is only as good as the shares. A cross-sectional shock
contributes no time variation, so the case rests on why firms ended up with the shares
they had. Here the argument is historical: networks formed before 2010 for reasons
unrelated to AI, which the anticipation and pre-growth tests support.

Second, build exposure to the correlated attributes with the same shares. Most
plausible violations of the exclusion restriction involve the shock being correlated
with another attribute of the same units, here computer science strength and prestige.
Computing exposure to those attributes from the same shares and controlling for it
removes the most likely alternative explanation.

Third, a binary shock built from percentile cutoffs is fragile at the margin.
Four of 48 universities change status under a reasonable reconstruction of the rule.
The authors' robustness tables use a continuous research-strength measure from
csrankings.org, an earlier 2000–2004 window, and drop Stanford, CMU, and Illinois one
at a time. That is the right response: show that the estimate does not depend on which
side of the cutoff the marginal units fall.

## Regression Discontinuity {#sec-causal-rd}

A **regression discontinuity** design exploits rules that assign treatment based on
whether a continuous **running variable** crosses a known **cutoff**. A customer
becomes a "gold-tier" member at 1,000 loyalty points; a buyer earns free shipping
at a \$50 basket; an ad campaign targets ZIP codes above a median-income
threshold. Units just below and just above the cutoff are, in every respect other
than treatment, nearly identical—their assignment is determined by a sliver of the
running variable that is plausibly as good as random. Comparing outcomes just above
versus just below the threshold therefore identifies the treatment effect *at the
cutoff*.

Let $X_i$ be the running variable, $c$ the cutoff, and treatment $D_i = \mathbf{1}\{X_i \geq c\}$
in the **sharp** design. The estimand is the jump in the conditional expectation of
the outcome at the cutoff,

$$
\tau_{\text{RD}}
= \lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x]
- \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x].
$$ {#eq-47-rd}

In practice $\tau_{\text{RD}}$ is estimated by fitting flexible regressions—usually
**local linear** regressions within a bandwidth $h$ around $c$—separately on each
side and reading off the gap at $c$. In the **fuzzy** design, crossing the cutoff
changes the *probability* of treatment rather than treatment itself; the jump in
outcomes is then scaled by the jump in treatment probability, making fuzzy RD a
local IV with cutoff-crossing as the instrument.

**Identifying assumption: continuity.** RD identifies the effect at the cutoff if
the potential outcomes $\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid X_i = x]$ and
$\mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) \mid X_i = x]$ are **continuous** in $x$ at $c$—that is, nothing
*other* than treatment jumps at the threshold. Then any discontinuity in the
observed outcome must be caused by the treatment.

**What breaks identification.** The fatal threat is **manipulation** of the running
variable: if units can precisely control which side of the cutoff they land on—a
customer nudging a basket to exactly \$50, a salesperson booking revenue to clear a
quota—then those who sort just above the cutoff differ systematically from those
just below, and continuity fails. The standard diagnostic is the **McCrary density
test**: a discontinuity in the *density* of $X$ at $c$ signals sorting. Two further
practices guard validity: confirm that pre-determined covariates do *not* jump at
the cutoff (a placebo RD on baseline characteristics), and show the estimate is
robust to bandwidth choice, since RD trades bias (wide bandwidth, more
extrapolation) against variance (narrow bandwidth, fewer observations). The estimand
is also intrinsically **local**: RD recovers the effect only at $c$ and need not
generalize to units far from the threshold.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(47)

# Running variable: loyalty points. Treatment at >= 1000. Smooth baseline
# relationship between points and spending PLUS a true jump of 8 at the cutoff.
n <- 4000; cutoff <- 1000; true_jump <- 8
points  <- runif(n, 600, 1400)
D       <- as.integer(points >= cutoff)
spend   <- 20 + 0.03 * (points - cutoff) + true_jump * D + rnorm(n, 0, 4)

# Local linear RD within a bandwidth, separate slopes each side.
h <- 150
inb <- abs(points - cutoff) <= h
rd_fit <- lm(spend ~ D + I(points - cutoff) + D:I(points - cutoff),
             data = data.frame(spend, D, points), subset = inb)
jump_hat <- coef(rd_fit)["D"]
cat(sprintf("True jump at cutoff: %.3f\n", true_jump))
#> True jump at cutoff: 8.000
cat(sprintf("RD estimate:         %.3f\n", jump_hat))
#> RD estimate:         8.899

s <- sample(n, 400)
plot(points[s], spend[s], pch = 16, col = "grey70", cex = 0.6,
     xlab = "Loyalty points (running variable)", ylab = "Spending")
abline(v = cutoff, lty = 3)
gl <- seq(cutoff - h, cutoff, length.out = 50)
gr <- seq(cutoff, cutoff + h, length.out = 50)
predl <- predict(rd_fit, data.frame(D = 0, points = gl))
predr <- predict(rd_fit, data.frame(D = 1, points = gr))
lines(gl, predl, lwd = 3); lines(gr, predr, lwd = 3)
```

The simulation is sharp; eligibility rules in the field rarely are.
@hotchkiss2026smallbiz supply a fuzzy design with every diagnostic on display.
Subchapter V, a streamlined bankruptcy procedure for small businesses, is open
only to debtors whose noncontingent liabilities do not exceed \$7.5 million.
But eligible firms may still choose traditional Chapter 11, and a dozen cases
above the line were admitted after courts classified some of their debts as
contingent, so crossing the cutoff shifts the *probability* of treatment. Firms
just below it are 41.9 percentage points more likely to use the procedure
(first-stage $F = 71.23$). Scaling the jump in plan confirmations by that first
stage gives a 32.0-point increase within \$4 to \$11 million of liabilities and
49.5 points within \$6 to \$9 million, where identification is most credible
but the first-stage $F$ falls to 19.71.

Three features are worth copying. The running variable was not in the
administrative data: reported total liabilities include contingent and
unliquidated claims that do not count toward eligibility, so the authors
hand-collected each debtor's schedules of claims to measure it. The validity
checks are the full set described above: a McCrary test ($p = 0.25$), six
covariates smooth individually and jointly, a donut that drops cases between
\$7 and \$7.5 million, second-order polynomials, and a placebo cutoff at \$4
million. And the threat specific to this setting is not manipulation but entry,
since a more generous procedure could change which firms file at all; the
authors bound that possibility rather than assume it away
(@sec-ent-bankruptcy). The same reform also supports a
difference-in-differences comparison with pre-2020 filings. Its 12.5-point
intent-to-treat estimate, divided by the 0.42 first stage, implies roughly 30
points, so two designs resting on different assumptions arrive at nearly the
same local effect.

### Stacked Discontinuities: Unbundling Two Policies at One Cutoff {#sec-causal-rd-stacked}

Regulation rarely changes one thing at a time. A consumer-protection law that
standardizes a product usually also rewrites how its price is disclosed, so a single
RD at the eligibility cutoff identifies the bundle, not either part. When the
components arrive at different dates, the same cutoff can be read in several periods
and the parts recovered by differencing. @kulkarni2026fineprint do this for consumer
loans in Chile.

Two laws set up the design. Law 20.448 (2011) created the Universal Credit Contract: for
consumer loans below 1,000 UF (*Unidad de Fomento*, an inflation-indexed unit of
account), banks had to show prospective borrowers a standardized contract that limited
the fees that could be charged and disclosed costs in a uniform format. Borrowers could
still take a different loan. Law 20.555 (2012) then extended the disclosure rules to
all loans, while the standardized product stayed below the cutoff only. Reading the
1,000-UF line in each period gives three discontinuities:

| Period | Below 1,000 UF | Above 1,000 UF | Jump at the cutoff identifies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Before 2011 | Nothing | Nothing | Any pre-existing jump (placebo) |
| 2011 | Standardization + disclosure | Nothing | Bundle + pre-existing jump |
| From 2012 | Standardization + disclosure | Disclosure | Standardization + pre-existing jump |

: The multi-stage design of @kulkarni2026fineprint. Each period's discontinuity, net of the pre-period one, identifies a different component; the difference between the 2011 and post-2012 jumps identifies disclosure. {#tbl-rd-stacked}

Subtracting the pre-period jump from each later one is a **difference-in-discontinuities**
[@grembi2016fiscal]. It removes anything else that happens at 1,000 UF, such as banks
pricing round amounts differently, as long as that other jump is stable over time. The
manipulation threat is unusually weak here. Loans are written in pesos, the cutoff is in
UF, and the exchange rate moves daily, so a borrower aiming at a peso amount cannot
easily land on a chosen side of the UF line. The authors still show density tests on
both scales. Two further tools address the locality of RD: a Cox hazard model estimated
around the cutoff, and the conditional-independence approach of
@angrist2015wanna, which uses covariates to extrapolate the effect away from the
cutoff.

The data are loan-level records of the Chilean financial regulator (CMF) for regulated
banks from 2009 to 2015. Disclosure reduces delinquency by 13.7 percentage points, a
40% fall, and default by 1.68 points, a 98% fall. Standardization has no effect. Disclosure does
not change initial loan terms, so it appears to work by improving borrowers'
understanding of what they owe, not by steering them to cheaper loans. For a marketer
this separates two levers that are usually pulled together: making a price legible
versus restricting what can be priced (@sec-nudges).

The simulation builds the three periods with a true disclosure effect of $-0.137$, a
zero standardization effect, and a small pre-existing jump at the cutoff that a
single-period RD would wrongly attribute to policy.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2011)

# Loan size in UF around the 1,000-UF cutoff; treatment applies BELOW it.
# Baseline delinquency ~0.34 with a smooth slope, plus a pre-existing jump
# of +0.03 just below 1,000 (e.g., bank practice at round amounts).
n_per  <- 30000; cutoff <- 1000; h <- 80
eff_D  <- -0.137; eff_S <- 0; pre_jump <- 0.03

sim_period <- function(period) {
  x     <- runif(n_per, 700, 1300)
  below <- as.integer(x < cutoff)
  D <- switch(period, pre = 0 * below, y2011 = below, post = rep(1L, n_per))
  S <- switch(period, pre = 0 * below, y2011 = below, post = below)
  p <- 0.34 + 0.0001 * (x - cutoff) + pre_jump * below + eff_D * D + eff_S * S
  data.frame(period, x, below, y = rbinom(n_per, 1, pmin(pmax(p, 0), 1)))
}

rd_jump <- function(d) {                  # local linear, separate slopes
  d <- d[abs(d$x - cutoff) <= h, ]
  coef(lm(y ~ below * I(x - cutoff), data = d))["below"]
}

periods <- c(pre = "pre", y2011 = "y2011", post = "post")
jumps   <- sapply(periods, function(p) unname(rd_jump(sim_period(p))))
bundle <- jumps["y2011"] - jumps["pre"]   # standardization + disclosure
stand  <- jumps["post"]  - jumps["pre"]   # standardization alone
disc   <- bundle - stand                  # disclosure alone

cat(sprintf("Naive 2011 RD (bundle + pre-jump): %6.3f\n", jumps["y2011"]))
#> Naive 2011 RD (bundle + pre-jump): -0.093
cat(sprintf("Bundle, diff-in-disc:              %6.3f  (true %6.3f)\n", bundle, eff_D + eff_S))
#> Bundle, diff-in-disc:              -0.125  (true -0.137)
cat(sprintf("Standardization alone:             %6.3f  (true %6.3f)\n", stand, eff_S))
#> Standardization alone:              0.008  (true  0.000)
cat(sprintf("Disclosure alone:                  %6.3f  (true %6.3f)\n", disc, eff_D))
#> Disclosure alone:                  -0.134  (true -0.137)
```
:::


The disclosure estimate is a difference of two differences, so it carries the sampling
error of four local regressions; with real data the confidence interval should come
from a joint bootstrap, not from adding standard errors.

The public replication package [@kulkarni2026fineprintdata] is a model of
documentation even though the microdata are confidential and must be requested from the
CMF. Three details are worth copying. The paper's bandwidths (82 UF for the main 2011
regressions) are fixed as named globals, with a switch to recompute MSE-optimal
bandwidths, so a replicator can tell exact replication from a robustness check. The
`rdrobust` version is pinned, because later builds move the optimal bandwidth in the
third decimal, which shifts weighted coefficients enough to flip a significance star.
And a crosswalk explains that the Chilean variable names for delinquency and default are
the reverse of the U.S. labels used in the paper. The spot check it reports, a 2011
coefficient of $-0.144$ (SE 0.070, $N = 1{,}117$) on ever-delinquent for borrowers who
saw the contract, is the bundle; it sits close to the disclosure-only estimate, as a
null standardization effect implies. The article has a corrigendum
[@kulkarni2026fineprintcorr], which should be read with it.

### Boundary Discontinuities: When the Running Variable Is a Place {#sec-causal-rd-boundary}

The loyalty-points example has a running variable that each unit carries as a
number. A large and growing class of designs replaces it with **geography**: the
treatment changes at an administrative line—a state border, a school-district
boundary, a media-market edge, a judicial-circuit line—and units are compared
according to which side of the line they fall on. These are **boundary** (or
spatial, or geographic) **discontinuity** designs, and they follow the same
identification logic as @eq-47-rd with the running variable replaced by signed
distance to the boundary.

The appeal is that economic geography is continuous and administrative geography
is not. Two adjacent counties share a labor market, weather, commuting patterns,
input prices, and regional demand shocks. If a policy, a tax, a regulation, or a
legal regime switches on at the line between them, the pair supplies a comparison
in which nearly everything except the treatment is held fixed by proximity. In
practice the estimator is usually not a single local linear fit but a
**contiguous-pair** regression: each treated unit is matched to the unit it
physically borders, and pair fixed effects absorb the shared local conditions.

@canayaz2026judges is a clean instance. Federal appellate circuits partition the
United States, and their boundaries cut through continuous economic geography.
Comparing a county's small business count to that of the county it borders, when
the two sit in different circuits, the authors find that a one-standard-deviation
shift toward less probusiness judicial ideology predicts a 1% reduction in firm
count—an effect that operates through the exit of young firms rather than through
relocation. The substantive reading is developed in @sec-ent-legal.

The setting also illustrates why a *static* cross-border comparison would not have
sufficed. Federal circuits are built from whole states, so every circuit boundary
is also a state boundary and carries the entire apparatus of state tax, licensing,
and incorporation law with it. What makes the design work is that the treatment
moves *along a fixed boundary over time*: circuit ideology turns over as judges
are appointed and replaced for reasons unconnected to any one county's economy, so
a county-pair effect absorbs the permanent differences between the two states and
identification comes from within-pair change. The residual threat is not static
state policy but state policy that *changes* in a way correlated with the timing
of judicial turnover—a much narrower claim to have to rule out, and the general
lesson for any boundary design whose treatment has a time dimension.

**What breaks identification here is different from what breaks a score-based
RD.** Manipulation of the running variable, the fatal threat in @sec-causal-rd, is
mostly irrelevant: a firm cannot nudge its county across a circuit line, and the
paper's finding that the effect runs through exit rather than relocation is
itself evidence that sorting is not driving it. Three other threats take its
place, and they are the ones to interrogate.

- **Coincident boundaries.** The identifying assumption is that *only* the
  treatment changes at the line. Administrative boundaries are notoriously
  nested: judicial circuits largely follow state lines, and state lines also
  carry tax rates, licensing rules, minimum wages, incorporation law, and
  Medicaid eligibility. A discontinuity estimated at such a line recovers the
  effect of the *bundle*, not of the component the researcher has in mind.
  Boundaries that cut *within* states, or variation in the treatment's intensity
  over time along a fixed boundary, are the standard escapes.
- **Spillovers across the line.** RD assumes the untreated side reveals the
  treated side's counterfactual. Adjacency makes that assumption harder, not
  easier: workers commute, customers cross, and firms on the control side may be
  affected by the treatment through exactly the proximity that makes them a good
  comparison. A treatment effect that leaks across the boundary biases the
  estimate toward zero.
- **Boundary endogeneity and sample size.** Some boundaries were drawn *because*
  of a pre-existing economic difference, which violates continuity at the moment
  of drawing. And because only units near the line are usable, effective sample
  size falls sharply with the bandwidth; standard errors must also be clustered
  in a way that respects spatial correlation, since neighboring units'
  disturbances are not independent.

For marketing, the natural applications sit where a firm's decision environment
switches at a line the customer does not perceive: designated market areas for
advertising exposure, state-level privacy and advertising-disclosure regimes
(@sec-privacy), sales-tax nexus rules for e-commerce, and franchise or
distribution territories. In each case the design's credibility rests on the same
question—what *else* changes at that boundary—rather than on any statistical
diagnostic.

### Algorithmic Discontinuities: When the Running Variable Is a Ranking Score {#sec-causal-rd-algorithmic}

Loyalty tiers and liability caps are rules someone wrote into a contract. A
platform's ranking code is also a rule, applied millions of times a day, and
wherever it sorts items by a continuous score it creates a cutoff at every
boundary between two adjacent items. @narayanan2015 exploited this in search
advertising, where an auction's ad rank sets each ad's position
(@sec-mmm-advertising). @moehring2026reddit carries the idea into a social-media
feed, and the case shows what an algorithm-made discontinuity can and cannot
deliver.

The question is how much a post's position in the feed of Reddit's politics
community raises the comments it receives. The naive comparison is confounded
in the usual way: inherently more commentable posts collect more upvotes, upvotes
move them up the feed, and they would have drawn more comments wherever they sat.
The source of exogeneity is the platform's own code. Until 2017 Reddit kept an
open-source mirror of its code base, so the default "hot" ranking can be read
off exactly. Each post receives the score

$$
s_{jt} = \operatorname{sign}(v_{jt})\,\log_{10}\!\big(\max\{|v_{jt}|,\,1\}\big)
- \frac{a_{jt}}{45{,}000},
$$ {#eq-47-reddit-hot}

where $v_{jt}$ is the post's net upvotes and $a_{jt}$ its age in seconds, and
the feed lists posts in descending order of $s_{jt}$. To hold its score, a post must
gain a factor of ten in net votes every 12.5 hours. For two posts competing for
positions $r$ and $r+1$, the running variable is the score difference
$\Delta s_i = s_i - s_{-i}$. Treatment is being listed above the rival, and it
switches on as $\Delta s_i$ crosses zero. The identifying assumption is the usual
continuity: a post's latent commentability does not jump at $\Delta s_i = 0$.
Several features make that assumption credible. The cutoff is relative, not
absolute. Two noisy vote streams and two clocks decide which of a particular
pair of posts leads at the moment a snapshot is taken. A post that edges its
rival by a few hundredths of a log-vote should be no more interesting than one
that trails by the same margin.

Four implementation choices are worth copying.

- **The running variable is rebuilt from outside the platform.** Feed positions,
  vote scores, ages, and publisher domains come from Internet Archive snapshots
  of the community's first page (the top 25 posts). Comments come from a public
  archive of Reddit activity. Because the code mirror was not maintained after
  early 2017, the analysis stops in 2016; the rule has to be the one actually in
  force.
- **The score has two dimensions.** $\Delta s_i$ combines a vote difference and an
  age difference, so the cutoff is a frontier in that plane, as with the boundary
  designs above (@sec-causal-rd-boundary). The effect is estimated at the origin,
  where the two posts are balanced on both votes and age.
- **The first stage falls short of one, and a donut handles it.** Reddit adds
  noise to displayed vote counts to deter manipulation and caches rankings for
  speed, so a reconstructed score sometimes disagrees with the order on screen.
  Noise in a running variable misclassifies units precisely at the cutoff.
  Following @dong2023measurement, the author drops pairs with
  $|\Delta s_i| < 0.05$. The mismatch that remains is flat in $\Delta s_i$, which
  points to caching rather than vote noise, and the first-stage jump is close
  to one at most boundaries.
- **Estimation is local, then smoothed.** Each of the 24 boundaries gets a
  quasi-Poisson regression with a linear term in $\Delta s_i$ on each side and a
  uniform kernel. The bandwidth is the mean-squared-error-optimal choice
  [@calonico2014robust], and standard errors are clustered by snapshot. Because
  rank-by-rank estimates are noisy, a stacked regression then imposes
  $\tau_r = \tau_0 + \tau_1 \log r$.

The validity evidence follows the standard pattern. Placebo RDs on pre-treatment
covariates (publisher slant, vote score, post age, hour posted) are nearly all
insignificant at the 5% level. Estimates are stable across bandwidths, donut
widths, comment windows, and polynomial orders. No density test is reported.
Sorting here would mean steering one's post past a specific rival at the moment
of an archive snapshot, which is a different and much less plausible threat
than a customer topping up a basket to a free-shipping threshold.

The results show how much the naive comparison overstates position effects. In
the author's April 2026 manuscript, moving from second to first place raises
comments in the following hour by 58.1% (a smoothed top-boundary effect of
0.458 log points, standard error 0.058). The effect decays with depth: the
estimated slope on $\log r$ is $-0.164$. The naive comparison at the top boundary is 0.790, while
the rank-specific RD is 0.507. Below the first position the naive and RD
estimates are close. The author's reading is that each hour has a top story
that would have led engagement anywhere on the page. The same pattern, a naive
estimate inflated mainly at the top, appears in Expedia's randomized hotel
rankings [@ursu2018power]. (The 2024 draft on OSF used a log(1 + comments)
outcome over 20 minutes and reported a 42.5% top-slot effect. Numbers here
follow the later manuscript and should be checked against the published
article.)

The RD is not the end of the paper. Its estimates become the exposure
parameters of a comment-choice model (@sec-sm-rd-structure), which is then used
to evaluate rankings Reddit never ran (@sec-platform-governance). The
simulation below builds the design in miniature. Latent quality drives both
upvotes and comments, the hot score of @eq-47-reddit-hot assigns the top slot,
and displayed votes carry a little noise.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(4707)

# --- A feed snapshot, reduced to the contest for the top slot ----------------
# Each period, two posts compete for position 1. Latent "commentability" q
# drives upvotes, so the better post tends to win the slot AND to draw comments
# anyway: the selection problem that makes a naive rank comparison misleading.
n_per <- 20000
q1  <- rnorm(n_per); q2 <- rnorm(n_per)
votes <- function(q) round(10^(2.6 + 0.35 * q + rnorm(length(q), 0, 0.35)))
v1 <- votes(q1); v2 <- votes(q2)
age1 <- runif(n_per, 1, 14) * 3600; age2 <- runif(n_per, 1, 14) * 3600

# Reddit's (pre-2017) "hot" score: log10 votes minus age / 45,000 seconds
hot <- function(v, a) sign(v) * log10(pmax(abs(v), 1)) - a / 45000
D   <- as.integer(hot(v1, age1) > hot(v2, age2))   # post 1 ranked first?

# Comments in the next window: the true effect of the top slot is tau
tau  <- 0.40                                      # log points, about +49%
cred <- plogis(0.8 * q1 + rnorm(n_per))           # publisher credibility, pre-treatment
y1   <- rpois(n_per, exp(1.2 + 0.6 * q1 + tau * D))

# The researcher sees vote counts with display noise, so the running variable
# is measured with error near zero; a 0.05 donut removes the misclassified band.
v1_obs <- round(v1 * exp(rnorm(n_per, 0, 0.03)))
v2_obs <- round(v2 * exp(rnorm(n_per, 0, 0.03)))
ds <- hot(v1_obs, age1) - hot(v2_obs, age2)

# --- (1) Naive: compare outcomes of the top-ranked and second-ranked post ------
naive <- coef(glm(y1 ~ D, family = quasipoisson))["D"]

# --- (2) Local RD: quasi-Poisson, linear in the running variable each side -----
rd <- function(y, h = 0.5, donut = 0.05, cut = 0, fam = quasipoisson()) {
  x  <- ds - cut; dd <- as.integer(x > 0)
  ok <- abs(x) <= h & abs(x) >= donut
  unname(coef(glm(y ~ dd * x, family = fam, subset = ok))["dd"])
}
fs <- rd(D, fam = gaussian())                     # first stage: jump in P(top)

out <- c(true_tau          = tau,
         naive_rank_gap    = unname(naive),
         rd_estimate       = rd(y1),
         rd_no_donut       = rd(y1, donut = 0),
         rd_wide_bw        = rd(y1, h = 1.0),
         rd_narrow_bw      = rd(y1, h = 0.25),
         first_stage       = fs,
         first_stage_no_donut = rd(D, donut = 0, fam = gaussian()),
         balance_cred      = rd(cred, fam = gaussian()),
         balance_latent_q  = rd(q1,   fam = gaussian()),
         placebo_cut_0.6   = rd(y1, h = 0.4, cut = 0.6))
round(out, 3)
#>             true_tau       naive_rank_gap          rd_estimate 
#>                0.400                0.804                0.377 
#>          rd_no_donut           rd_wide_bw         rd_narrow_bw 
#>                0.345                0.376                0.358 
#>          first_stage first_stage_no_donut         balance_cred 
#>                1.000                0.871               -0.002 
#>     balance_latent_q      placebo_cut_0.6 
#>               -0.033                0.002
```
:::


The naive gap between first- and second-placed posts (0.804) is twice the true
effect (0.400), because the same latent quality that wins the slot also draws
comments. The local RD gives 0.377, and widening or narrowing the bandwidth
moves it little (0.376 and 0.358). Remove the donut and two things happen
together. Display noise misclassifies near-ties, the first stage drops from
1.000 to 0.871, and the estimate is pulled toward zero (0.345), which is the
attenuation @dong2023measurement warn about. The balance rows show what
continuity means. Publisher credibility does not jump at the cutoff, and
neither does latent quality, which no real study can observe; that is why
papers check balance on the covariates they do observe. A placebo cutoff at
$\Delta s = 0.6$, where nothing happens, returns zero.

### Rank Cutoffs: Medals on a Leaderboard {#sec-causal-rd-medals}

A feed creates a cutoff between every pair of adjacent posts. A contest leaderboard
has only a few, and the platform announces them in advance. Kaggle, the
machine-learning competition site, awards bronze, silver and gold medals by final
rank. @liu2026goldmedals use the gold line to ask what a purely symbolic award does
to the winner afterwards. Gold medallists enter fewer later contests and contribute
more to the community: they post more often, write longer posts, receive more
upvotes and share more code. Bronze and silver medals have no detectable effect. The
authors call this goal shifting. The award moves effort out of the activity it
rewards and into other kinds of platform engagement. Earlier field evidence on
symbolic awards concerned the rewarded activity itself; in a natural field
experiment, randomly assigned awards raised retention among new Wikipedia editors
[@gallus2017symbolic].

The running variable $r_{ij}$ is contestant $i$'s signed rank distance from the gold
cutoff in contest $j$, and treatment is $\mathbf{1}\{r_{ij} \geq 0\}$. Every
specification carries contest fixed effects and fixed effects for the contestant's
Kaggle progression tier. Three features of the setting are worth copying.

- **The platform hides the running variable until it is too late to sort.** During
  a contest, Kaggle scores submissions on a public leaderboard that uses part of the
  test data. Final ranks come from a private, held-out part. Among the top 10 on the
  public board, the correlation between public and final rank is 0.004, and among
  the top 50 it is 0.015. A contestant near the gold line cannot tell which side of
  it they will finish on. This is the substantive argument against manipulation,
  and it is stronger than a density test, because it explains why sorting cannot
  happen.
- **The other two medal lines are built-in placebos.** The same contestants, rules
  and outcome measures apply at the silver and bronze cutoffs. Null effects there
  mean the gold result is not about winning *a* medal, or about the attention any
  medal brings.
- **Money can be separated from the medal.** Some top finishers also win cash.
  Dropping winners who received prize money leaves the estimates almost unchanged
  (participation −0.042, posting probability 0.170), and so does keeping only
  contests that offer money or only featured contests.

The appendix is unusually candid about one weakness. The estimates move with the
bandwidth, and they move in one direction. As the bandwidth widens from 0.5 to 2.0,
the participation effect shrinks from −0.072 to −0.043, while the posting-probability
effect grows from 0.069 to 0.165 and the post-length effect from 0.454 to 1.056. The
authors attribute this to smoothing bias. A local linear fit is a good approximation
only close to the cutoff, and a wider window brings in ranks where the conditional
mean bends. Global polynomials show the same instability more sharply: the
posting-probability jump is 0.225 with a second-order polynomial and 0.095 with a
fifth-order one. Two things survive every variant. Every specification gives the
same sign. And the participation effect, between −0.035 and −0.072, is far more
stable than the posting effects. The safe reading is the sign and the
narrow-bandwidth magnitude. The rest of the robustness table is consistent:
rectangular and Epanechnikov kernels, local quadratic fits, added controls for ten
pre-award covariates, and logit and Poisson versions all give the same signs. The
appendix's own code measures are weaker than the posting ones. The number of
scripts rises (0.028, SE 0.013), but script versions and lines of code do not move
significantly.

Two further designs answer different questions from the RD:

- **Local randomization.** Treating the five teams on each side of the line as if
  randomly assigned [@cattaneo2024extensions], participation falls from 0.192 to
  0.146 (Fisher $p = 0.019$) and posting probability rises from 0.448 to 0.617. This
  view needs no functional form at all, which matters given the drift above.
- **Silver medallists as controls.** A difference-in-differences design compares
  first-time gold medallists with silver medallists who have never won gold,
  following @foerderer2021winner, over 325,717 user-weeks with user, contest and week
  fixed effects. Participation falls by 0.091 and posting probability rises by
  0.055. This is an average over all gold winners, not the effect at the line, which
  is why the participation drop is twice the RD estimate. The event study shows flat
  pre-trends, a participation drop that persists, and a posting spike that settles
  above its earlier level rather than returning to it.

A last check comes from the platform's history. When Kaggle introduced medals in
June 2016, it awarded them retroactively for 156 earlier contests (1,518 gold and
4,505 silver medallists). These medals came as a surprise, and the same
gold-versus-silver comparison finds no effect on anything: participation 0.012 (SE
0.009) on 109,950 user-weeks. The authors read this as evidence that the effect
needs an *anticipated* award, and say the result is suggestive only. A reader should
weigh it lower still. Many recipients of a medal for a contest years earlier had
probably left the platform, so a null could reflect absence rather than
indifference.

On mechanism, the published paper draws on self-determination theory and the
needs-as-motives hypothesis. A gold medal satisfies the need for competence that
drove the competing, and effort moves to contributing. Nine gold medallists,
interviewed in August 2025, describe gold as proof of ability and as release from
competing. One Grandmaster adds that competition golds carry far more prestige than
the golds awarded for code or discussion. The effects differ across winners.
Winners with more previous competition medals shift more toward contributing, those
with more contribution medals add less, and team winners shift less than solo
winners. The working-paper version explained the same pattern with downward social
comparison instead. For a marketer, the design raises a question about status
programs such as loyalty tiers (@sec-rel-loyalty). Reaching the top tier may change
behaviour outside the rewarded activity, such as reviews, referrals and help to
other customers, as much as inside it. A program that measures only spending would
miss that shift.

The simulation below builds the design. Leaderboards have three medal lines, only
gold changes behaviour, and baseline posting drops off steeply between ranks 15 and
35, so the fit below the gold line bends as the window widens.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2016)

# --- Leaderboards with three medal lines -------------------------------------
# 5,000 contests with 100 ranked teams each. Only GOLD (top 10) changes
# behaviour; silver (top 30) and bronze (top 60) are labels with no effect.
# Baseline posting falls off steeply between ranks 15 and 35, so the outcome
# curves away from a straight line as the window widens below the gold line.
n_contest <- 5000; n_team <- 100
rank <- rep(1:n_team, n_contest)                       # 1 = winner
cut  <- c(gold = 10, silver = 30, bronze = 60)         # last place inside each medal
tau_post <- 0.10; tau_comp <- -0.045                   # true effects of gold

gold <- as.integer(rank <= cut[["gold"]])
post <- rbinom(length(rank), 1, 0.15 + 0.35 * plogis((25 - rank) / 5) + tau_post * gold)
comp <- rbinom(length(rank), 1, 0.30 + 0.05 * exp(-rank / 40) + tau_comp * gold)

r_to <- function(k) (cut[[k]] + 0.5 - rank) / 10       # rank distance in 10s, > 0 inside

# Local polynomial RD, triangular kernel, separate fits on each side.
rd <- function(y, k, h, p = 1) {
  x <- r_to(k); w <- pmax(0, 1 - abs(x) / h); d <- as.integer(x > 0)
  unname(coef(lm(y ~ d * poly(x, p, raw = TRUE), weights = w, subset = w > 0))["d"])
}

bw  <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3)
tab <- rbind(posting_linear    = sapply(bw, function(h) rd(post, "gold", h)),
             posting_quadratic = sapply(bw, function(h) rd(post, "gold", h, p = 2)),
             contest_linear    = sapply(bw, function(h) rd(comp, "gold", h)))
colnames(tab) <- paste0("h=", bw)
round(tab, 3)
#>                    h=0.5    h=1  h=1.5    h=2    h=3
#> posting_linear     0.090  0.086  0.079  0.069  0.060
#> posting_quadratic  0.110  0.090  0.093  0.093  0.076
#> contest_linear    -0.061 -0.053 -0.054 -0.055 -0.054

# The silver and bronze lines are built-in placebos.
round(c(posting_at_silver = rd(post, "silver", 1), posting_at_bronze = rd(post, "bronze", 1)), 3)
#> posting_at_silver posting_at_bronze 
#>            -0.001             0.000

# Local randomization: the 5 places either side of the gold line, with a
# Fisher p-value from permuting the medal label inside that window.
win  <- abs(r_to("gold")) <= 0.5
dm   <- function(y, d) mean(y[d == 1]) - mean(y[d == 0])
obs  <- dm(comp[win], gold[win])
perm <- replicate(2000, dm(comp[win], sample(gold[win])))
round(c(contest_diff_in_means = obs, fisher_p = mean(abs(perm) >= abs(obs))), 3)
#> contest_diff_in_means              fisher_p 
#>                -0.043                 0.000
```
:::


The true posting effect is 0.10. The local linear estimate starts near it (0.090 at
the narrowest bandwidth) and falls steadily to 0.060 as the window widens, the same
kind of one-directional drift as in the appendix. A local quadratic fit stays
closer to the truth over the middle bandwidths, at the cost of more noise. The
participation outcome has a nearly straight baseline, so its estimate moves little
across bandwidths. Note that the gold side of the line holds only ten ranks, so widening the
bandwidth adds data almost entirely from the losing side. The silver and bronze
lines return zero, as they should. The five-place local-randomization comparison
recovers the participation effect without fitting any curve.

## Synthetic Control {#sec-causal-scm}

Difference-in-differences needs a control group whose untreated trend matches the
treated group's. When the treated unit is a *single* large entity—one country where
a brand launched, one state that changed a privacy law, one market where a flagship
store opened—no single control unit is a credible match. The **synthetic control
method** constructs the counterfactual as a *weighted average* of untreated "donor"
units, choosing the weights so that the synthetic unit reproduces the treated
unit's pre-treatment outcome path (and predictors). The treatment effect is then the
gap between the treated unit and its synthetic twin after the intervention.

Let unit $1$ be treated at time $T_0$ and units $2,\dots,J+1$ be the donor pool.
Choose nonnegative weights $\mathbf{w} = (w_2,\dots,w_{J+1})$, with
$\sum_j w_j = 1$, to minimize pre-treatment discrepancy,

$$
\mathbf{w}^{\star} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}}
\sum_{t < T_0}\Big(Y_{1t} - \sum_{j=2}^{J+1} w_j\,Y_{jt}\Big)^2,
\quad w_j \geq 0,\ \textstyle\sum_j w_j = 1.
$$ {#eq-scm-weights}

The estimated effect at each post-period is the gap between the treated unit and
the weighted donors,

$$
\hat\tau_{1t} = Y_{1t} - \sum_{j=2}^{J+1} w_j^{\star}\,Y_{jt},
\qquad t \geq T_0.
$$ {#eq-scm-effect}

**Identifying assumptions.** SCM identifies the treated unit's ATT if (i) the
weighted donors reproduce the treated unit's *pre-treatment* outcomes closely
(good pre-fit), (ii) the donors are themselves untreated and free of spillovers
from the treatment, and (iii) the relationship that made the synthetic control
track the treated unit before treatment *continues to hold* absent treatment—the
synthetic-control analogue of parallel trends, but enforced on the full
pre-period path rather than a single trend. The convexity constraints
($w_j \geq 0$, summing to one) prevent extrapolation outside the donor support and
make the weights interpretable.

**What breaks identification.** Poor pre-treatment fit is disqualifying: if the
synthetic unit cannot track the treated unit *before* the intervention, the
post-period gap is not credibly causal. **Interpolation bias** arises when donors
are too dissimilar from the treated unit; **overfitting** to noise inflates
apparent effects when the pre-period is short. Because there is only one treated
unit, inference rests not on large-sample theory but on **placebo (permutation)
tests**: reassign the treatment to each donor in turn, compute the placebo gap, and
ask whether the true treated unit's post/pre gap ratio is extreme relative to the
placebo distribution.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(47)

# One treated market + 20 donors over 30 periods; a brand campaign starts at t=21
# and lifts the treated market's sales by a growing amount.
Tn <- 30; T0 <- 20; J <- 20; true_post_effect <- 6
common <- cumsum(rnorm(Tn, 0.2, 0.4))                 # shared latent trend
donors <- sapply(1:J, function(j)
  3 + runif(1, 0.5, 1.5) * common + rnorm(Tn, 0, 0.6))
# Treated market is a convex blend of three donors, pre-treatment.
truew <- numeric(J); truew[c(2, 5, 11)] <- c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)
treated <- as.numeric(donors %*% truew) + rnorm(Tn, 0, 0.4)
treated[(T0 + 1):Tn] <- treated[(T0 + 1):Tn] +
  true_post_effect * seq_len(Tn - T0) / (Tn - T0)

# Solve for nonnegative weights summing to 1 on the PRE period via a simple
# projected optimization (quadratic loss, simplex constraint).
pre <- 1:T0
loss <- function(w) sum((treated[pre] - donors[pre, ] %*% w)^2)
ui <- rbind(diag(J), rep(-1, J)); ci <- c(rep(0, J), -1)  # w>=0, sum(w)<=1
w0 <- rep(0.9 / J, J)   # interior start: sum < 1, so constrOptim's strict-feasibility check passes
opt <- constrOptim(w0, loss, grad = NULL, ui = ui, ci = ci)
w <- opt$par / sum(opt$par)

synth <- as.numeric(donors %*% w)
gap_post <- mean(treated[(T0 + 1):Tn] - synth[(T0 + 1):Tn])
cat(sprintf("Mean post-period effect (truth ~%.2f): %.3f\n",
            true_post_effect / 2, gap_post))
#> Mean post-period effect (truth ~3.00): 3.313

plot(1:Tn, treated, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "Period", ylab = "Sales",
     ylim = range(c(treated, synth)))
lines(1:Tn, synth, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "firebrick")
abline(v = T0 + 0.5, lty = 3)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2),
       col = c("black", "firebrick"),
       legend = c("treated market", "synthetic control"))
```
